taxonomy_basis.summary: Soltis 2010 is used as the spine because it is the widely cited peer-reviewed review of African elephant vocal communication and explicitly summarizes the repertoire as perhaps nine acoustically distinct call types. Those inventory classes are represented here as rumble, roar, trumpet, snort, bark, grunt, rev, croak, and chuff. Contextual rumble forms such as contact, estrous, musth, bee-alarm, and human-alarm rumbles are treated as supported variants within rumble rather than separate call entries. Rare captive-derived classes are retained because they are part of the primary inventory, but their uncertainty and limited wild evidence are marked in the agreement labels.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-frequency, usually harmonic call with infrasonic fundamentals and context-dependent modulation, amplitude, duration, and formant structure. Rumbles can be nasal or oral, can occur singly or in exchanges, and grade into louder or noisier forms and combinations with higher-frequency calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used across the major documented low-frequency contexts, including long-distance contact and reunion, within-group coordination, close affiliative interaction, reproductive advertisement by estrous females and musth males, threat-specific alarm contexts, and infant care or begging situations. Receivers use rumble variation for social identity, reproductive assessment, danger assessment, and movement decisions.
calls.comments: Soltis 2010 lists rumbles as the most common and variable African elephant call class, while Poole et al. 1988, Wood et al. 2005, Stoeger et al. 2012, McComb et al. 2000, King et al. 2010, Soltis et al. 2014, and Pardo et al. 2024 all analyze rumbles in independent behavioral or acoustic datasets. Agreement is strong for the broad rumble class, even though sources split contextual variants differently.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, higher-frequency laryngeal call that can be noisy, tonal, or mixed, with extensive age- and arousal-related grading. Roars may occur alone or combined with rumbles, and infant roars have been separated into noisy, tonal, and mixed forms. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, broadband, noisy, tonal, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in high-arousal contexts such as distress, protest, suckling conflict, predator or social confrontation, intense excitement, and aggressive or defensive events. Calls by dependent young can recruit mothers or other family members, while adult roars are common in serious social or defensive episodes.
calls.comments: Roar is included in the Soltis 2010 inventory, Stoeger-Horwath et al. 2007 structurally separates infant roars and their subtypes, and Poole 2011 documents roar and roar-rumble forms in free-ranging Amboseli elephants. The broad call type is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud trunk-produced call with high-frequency energy, coarse harmonic or broadband structure, and strong modulation. Trumpets range from brief explosive blasts to more pulsated or nasal variants, and can grade in intensity with arousal. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, broadband, harmonic, short, loud, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during intense excitement, threat display, predator or human confrontation, charging, defensive bunching, social conflict, and play. Young elephants also produce trumpets in play or distress once they have enough motor control of the trunk.
calls.comments: Trumpet is one of the Soltis 2010 inventory classes and is independently recognized by Leong et al. 2003, Stoeger-Horwath et al. 2007, and Poole 2011. The broad trumpet class is strongly supported across captive, infant, and wild-context sources.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, sharp, broadband trunk exhalation produced by forcefully moving air through the trunk. It is acoustically more abrupt and signal-like than routine nasal clearing sounds, but may grade toward non-vocal blows. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, loud, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when elephants are alert, surprised, annoyed, socially excited, or confronting a possible threat. It can draw attention to a new situation and occur with vigilance or low-level threat display.
calls.comments: Snort is included in Soltis 2010 and Leong et al. 2003, and Poole 2011 and Stoeger and de Silva 2014 distinguish snorts from routine blows or sneezes. Existence agreement is strong for the broad trunk-call category.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, abrupt, higher-frequency call with noisy broadband energy that may occur alone or with a rumble component. Infant barks separate acoustically from rumbles, grunts, and roars in structural analyses, while wild-context descriptions treat bark-rumble forms as graded combinations. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, loud, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with protest, distress, high arousal, and agonistic or defensive situations, including young elephants' suckling or separation conflicts and broader wild contexts where bark-like calls combine with rumbles.
calls.comments: Soltis 2010 includes bark in the repertoire, Stoeger-Horwath et al. 2007 separates infant barks structurally, and Poole 2011 recognizes bark and bark-rumble forms in wild elephants. Agreement is medium because much of the quantitative evidence comes from infants and because bark-rumble combinations blur boundaries.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low, quiet laryngeal call that is structurally separated from infant rumbles, barks, and roars. Published descriptions emphasize very young calves and indicate a softer, less extended form than roars or rumbles. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Best supported for very young calves in close mother-infant contexts, including social interaction, nursing-related behavior, and low-arousal contact with caretaking adults. Adult use is not well established in the quantitative literature.
calls.comments: Soltis 2010 includes grunt in the inventory and Stoeger-Horwath et al. 2007 separates infant grunts in a quantitative infant repertoire. Poole 2011 also lists grunt among wild elephant acoustic signals. The label is medium because support is strongest for infants and much weaker for adult repertoire use.

calls.acoustic_description: A brief tonal harmonic call with a fundamental frequency higher than typical rumbles and a buzz-like or revving quality. It is often described as less than a second and may occur immediately before a rumble. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, short, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Reported rarely, mostly in captive classification work and in a small number of wild recordings without well-established behavioral context. Its function is therefore best treated as unresolved, possibly associated with close-range social attention or a learned/context-bound production.
calls.comments: Rev is retained because Soltis 2010 includes it and Leong et al. 2003 defined it acoustically, while Poole 2011 found only rare wild examples and no firm context. Stoeger and de Silva 2014 also treat rev as rare and difficult to compare across taxa. Agreement is weak.

calls.acoustic_description: A rare pulsatile call described as a croaking sound, often lasting longer than a rev and made of repeated low, rough pulses. Published accounts treat it as acoustically outside the common rumble, trumpet, snort, roar, bark, and grunt classes. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, long, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Known mainly from captive observations and rare wild or semi-wild discussions, with reported association to close-range activity rather than a well-established communicative function. It may be idiosyncratic or learned in some individuals.
calls.comments: Croak appears in the Soltis 2010 inventory and was described by Leong et al. 2003, but Poole 2011 and Stoeger and de Silva 2014 treat it as rare and possibly idiosyncratic or learned. Existence as a normal repertoire call is therefore weakly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, noisy exhalatory sound reported in captive acoustic classification. Later wild-context review describes similar sounds as possibly wheeze-like or sneeze-like rather than a clearly vocal call. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Included here only because the primary inventory retains it. Captive observations provide limited behavioral setting, while later wild-context work questions whether it is communicative or instead a respiratory byproduct.
calls.comments: Chuff is listed in the Soltis 2010 primary inventory via the Leong et al. 2003 captive classification, but Poole 2011 explicitly questions whether Leong's chuff is a cough, sneeze, or wheeze rather than a communicative call. Stoeger and de Silva 2014 also group chuff among rare, hard-to-compare signals. Existence agreement is weak.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Capranica 1968 is the species-specific repertoire spine because it explicitly enumerates the bullfrog vocal repertoire as mating call, three territorial-call subtypes, release call, warning call, and distress call. Later field, playback, endocrine, auditory, and defensive-vocalization studies refine acoustic and semantic detail while retaining every call type listed in this inventory.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, low-frequency, quasiharmonic call composed of one to many repeated croaks. Published descriptions identify the adult male advertisement call as a multicroak signal, commonly 1-12 croaks per call, with fine-temporal periodicity near 100 Hz, strong low-frequency energy around a few hundred hertz, and an additional higher spectral band in the low kilohertz range. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, loud, long, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males in breeding choruses. It attracts females, elicits vocal responses from other males, and mediates territorial neighbor-stranger recognition and spacing among resident males at calling sites.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 lists the mating call as a repertoire item, Wiewandt 1969 and Ryan 1980 document the call in field territorial and reproductive behavior, and Simmons 2004 plus Bee and Gerhardt 2001a/2002 analyze it in playback and recognition work. Terminology shifts between mating, advertisement, and mate call, but the call type itself is stable.

calls.acoustic_description: A curt, abrupt, low-frequency aggressive note. Later work equates the male encounter call with Wiewandt's bonk, describes it as spectrally similar to the advertisement call but much shorter, and places territorial-call energy in lower and middle frequency bands. Acoustic features: low frequency, harmonic, short, abrupt, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Emitted by territorial adult males during close-range male-male competition and defense of calling or shoreline territories. Field playback and model presentations show that males give this call when approaching or attacking apparent intruders.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 lists a male-only territorial call, Wiewandt 1969 describes the bonk during territorial playback and model experiments, and Simmons 2004 explicitly identifies the male encounter call as the bonk of Wiewandt. Terminology varies, but the male aggressive territorial call is independently supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A female-only territorial signal in Capranica's inventory. Later auditory work cites the female bullfrog territorial call as a broad-spectrum signal with low-frequency modulation, including steady modulation near 30 Hz followed by an abrupt upward glissando to about 90 Hz. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult females in territorial occupancy or trespass contexts. Capranica interpreted this female-specific type as alerting conspecifics that a defended area was occupied and being trespassed.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 explicitly lists a female-only territorial call and Fisher et al. 2011 independently refers to the female bullfrog territorial call when discussing behaviorally relevant acoustic modulation. The label is medium because there are fewer field-behavior studies of this female-specific subtype than of male territorial calling.

calls.acoustic_description: A territorial-call subtype made by both sexes in Capranica's inventory. It belongs to the bullfrog set of broad-spectrum, harmonically structured communication sounds with low-frequency temporal modulation, but later studies rarely isolate this shared subtype from male and female territorial calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, harmonic, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by both adult males and adult females in occupancy or trespass contexts. Capranica interpreted the territorial-call set as signals that a territory was occupied and that another frog was trespassing.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 explicitly lists a territorial subtype made by both sexes, so it is retained from the primary inventory. The label is weak because later field and playback literature usually collapses territorial signals into male encounter calls or advertisement-call aggression and does not independently resolve this shared subtype.

calls.acoustic_description: A repeated clasping-release vocalization with harmonic structure. Sonogram analysis found male and female release calls similar in duration, dominant-frequency characteristics, and secondary or tertiary harmonic display, although intercall intervals and call rates differ between the sexes; spectral-envelope work also shows strong peaks in the release-call spectrum. Acoustic features: harmonic, pulsed, short, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when an unreceptive female or a male is clasped by another male. The clasped animal struggles and emits the call, after which the amplexing frog releases it.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 lists release calls for both sexes, Boyd 1992 analyzes release calls and their hormonal control, Boyd 1997 summarizes release calling as a bullfrog sexual behavior, and Purgue 1997 records male release calls in sound-radiation experiments. These sources agree that the release call is a discrete call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A distinct natural call in the bullfrog repertoire with complex spectral and temporal structure. Capranica separated it from mating, territorial, release, and distress calls, and auditory-thalamus experiments found the warning call among the natural repertoire sounds that strongly stimulated both bullfrog auditory organs. Acoustic features: broadband, harmonic, short, abrupt, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by both sexes shortly before a leap into or out of water and sometimes after another call type. The context is startle or escape-related alerting rather than mating, territorial defense, or amplexus release.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 lists warning calls as a discrete call type, and Mudry and Capranica 1987 tested warning calls as one of the natural bullfrog repertoire sounds. The label is medium because later behavioral field studies rarely focus on this call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, high-pitched defensive call produced with the mouth open. Independent defensive-vocalization recordings describe long calls with many harmonic bands, dominant energy in the kilohertz range, and type-specific frequency contours that can include rises, falls, and nearly constant frequency portions. Acoustic features: high frequency, harmonic, loud, long, multi component, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by both sexes after repeated noxious stimulation, capture, or handling, especially in predator-like defensive contexts. The call is associated with open-mouth defensive display rather than breeding, territory defense, or amplexus release.
calls.comments: Capranica 1968 lists distress calls as part of the bullfrog repertoire, and Toledo and Haddad 2009 independently recorded and analyzed Lithobates catesbeianus distress calls among defensive vocalizations of anurans. This gives independent support beyond the primary inventory.

taxonomy_basis.summary: de Silva 2010 is used as the spine because it provides a quantitative wild inventory for Sri Lankan Asian elephants, classifying 3921 recorded vocalizations into eight single-call types, five combination-call types, and one rare musth-associated male call. Earlier wild observations by McKay 1973 and the independent southern India acoustic study by Nair et al. 2009 are used to strengthen broad categories such as rumble, roar, trumpet, and squeak/chirp, while de Silva-only splits are retained with cautious agreement labels. The non-vocal trunk-bounce signal described by de Silva is not included as a call entry.

calls.acoustic_description: A long, low-frequency harmonic vocalization with little energy above 500 Hz, lower fundamental frequency than rumbles, and relatively level frequency contours. It is usually soft to human listeners, often delivered in bouts or choruses, and may be barely audible beyond close range. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, long, quiet, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced across many social situations, especially while individuals are oriented toward an object or companion, moving, grazing alone, or interacting at close range. It can accompany following, approach, local coordination, and spacing among social groups.
calls.comments: de Silva 2010 separates growls from rumbles acoustically in a wild Sri Lankan inventory, and McKay 1973 used growl terminology in an earlier Sri Lankan account. Agreement is medium because Nair et al. 2009 grouped comparable low-frequency calls under rumbles rather than recognizing growl as a separate four-category class.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-frequency harmonic call with fundamental frequencies in the infrasonic or near-infrasonic range, longer duration than high-frequency calls, and variable frequency modulation. Compared with growls in the Sri Lankan inventory, rumbles have higher low-frequency fundamentals, more upper harmonic energy, stronger modulation, and greater carrying distance. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used for contact within and among herds, assembly before movement, close social interactions, group coordination in disorder or disturbance, between-herd encounters, and responses to other species or vehicles. Receivers may approach, gather, touch, orient, or coordinate movement after rumbles.
calls.comments: Rumble is recognized in the de Silva 2010 wild Sri Lankan inventory and in Nair et al. 2009 as one of four wild southern India call classes, with McKay 1973 describing related low-frequency sounds and Payne et al. 1986 documenting infrasonic calls in Asian elephants. The broad call type is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A brief high-frequency tonal call, commonly occurring in rapid bouts of three or more elements separated by less than a second. Typical elements have strongly modulated contours and correspond to the chirp category in other Asian elephant studies. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, short, repetitive, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly during disturbance, confusion, fear, or excitement, including encounters with humans, vehicles, other species, or a musth male. It can accompany bunching, confused running, orientation toward a possible source of threat, and separation from companions.
calls.comments: de Silva 2010 names this call squeak and explicitly equates it with the chirp terminology of McKay 1973 and Nair et al. 2009. Nair et al. 2009 independently classifies chirps as one of four wild southern India call categories, so the broad call type is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud high-frequency trunk call with harmonic structure, variable modulation, and occasional double-voicing. It is usually a short, conspicuous call and is acoustically distinct from squeaks and roars despite overlapping high-frequency energy. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, harmonic, loud, abrupt, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during disturbance, threat display, charging, object throwing, defensive agitation, play, and encounters with humans, vehicles, or other species. It can occur alone or with squeaks during high-arousal episodes.
calls.comments: Trumpet is included in de Silva 2010, Nair et al. 2009, and McKay 1973, making it one of the best-supported wild Asian elephant call categories.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, noisy, aperiodic or weakly harmonic call that overlaps high-frequency ranges with trumpets and squeaks but lacks their regular temporal and spectral patterning. In de Silva 2010 it is shorter than longroar and can occur singly or in bouts. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, loud, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during movement, disturbance, distress, play, arrival at places such as waterholes, arrival of other groups, and aggressive interactions. It is associated with high-arousal social or environmental events rather than a single narrow context.
calls.comments: Roar is recognized by de Silva 2010, Nair et al. 2009, and McKay 1973, though de Silva further splits longroars by duration. Agreement is strong for the broad roar category.

calls.acoustic_description: A longer noisy roar-like vocalization with aperiodic structure, resonant regions, and occasional partial harmonics. It can occur in long bouts by one caller or in choruses, and is acoustically separated from shorter roars mainly by duration. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly during separation, searching, movement, and distress, including cases in which a caller persists until joined by another individual. It can carry over long distances and may help re-establish contact or coordinate across obscured space.
calls.comments: de Silva 2010 separates longroars as a duration-based wild call type, while McKay 1973 recognized roars more broadly. Nair et al. 2009 uses a broader roar category, so the longroar split has medium agreement.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, non-repeated aperiodic call, shorter than roars and longroars. It is a brief broadband vocalization rather than a long tonal or modulated low-frequency call. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Given during group movement or in aggressive episodes with lunging, pushing, or biting, usually directed at other elephants and especially calves. Calves may also direct similar calls at other animals during play.
calls.comments: Bark is a named de Silva 2010 wild category, and de Silva notes possible correspondence with McKay 1973's ambiguous snort terminology. Nair et al. 2009 did not keep bark as a separate class, so agreement is medium rather than strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-frequency harmonic call longer than the typical squeak, with stronger frequency modulation and tonal structure. It is acoustically closer to squeak than to roar but differs in duration and contour. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, harmonic, long, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Recorded during rare high-arousal disturbance events, often in the same broad situations as squeaks. Available wild observations associate it with fear, excitement, or disturbance rather than routine contact.
calls.comments: de Silva 2010 lists squeals as a wild call type but also states they had not previously been described. The category is therefore weakly supported outside the primary inventory.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-part combination call with a short aperiodic bark-like leading segment followed by a lower-frequency rumble-like segment. The leading segment resembles single barks in duration, while the second segment overlaps more with rumbles than with growls. Acoustic features: multi component, broadband, noisy, low frequency, harmonic, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly during movement and searching, with occasional use by calves wanting to nurse. It appears to occur in high-attention coordination contexts where a short onset is joined to a low-frequency follow-on segment.
calls.comments: Bark-rumble is a named wild combination call in de Silva 2010, but de Silva notes that combination calls had not previously been recognized as such. Independent confirmation is lacking, so existence agreement is weak.

calls.acoustic_description: A combination call with a noisy roar-like leading segment followed by a lower-frequency rumble-like segment. The first segment is not significantly different in duration from single roars, and the second segment is acoustically closer to rumbles than to growls. Acoustic features: multi component, broadband, noisy, low frequency, harmonic, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced primarily during movement and searching, with occasional calf nursing-related use. It appears in contexts requiring coordination, contact, or renewed attention rather than in a single narrow behavioral setting.
calls.comments: Roar-rumble is part of the de Silva 2010 wild combination-call inventory, but the combination category lacks independent confirmation and may be functionally graded with related calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-part call with a long noisy roar-like leading segment followed by a lower-frequency rumble-like segment. The first component is long but shorter than stand-alone longroars, likely because it is joined to the second segment, and the second segment has a falling low-frequency contour. Acoustic features: multi component, broadband, noisy, low frequency, harmonic, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly during separation, movement, searching, and distress. It may serve long-distance contact or coordination when the caller is separated, moving, or attempting to locate companions.
calls.comments: Longroar-rumble is a frequent named combination type in de Silva 2010, but combination-call splitting has not been independently replicated. Agreement is medium because its components map onto better-known roar and rumble categories.

calls.acoustic_description: A combination call with a brief croak-like leading segment under one second followed by a rumble- or growl-like low-frequency segment. It occurs in bouts where rumbles are also present and multiple individuals may call rapidly. Acoustic features: multi component, tonal, short, low frequency, harmonic, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Recorded in chorused social bouts with rumbles, usually when two or more individuals called in rapid succession. Its documented use is in group-level social coordination rather than aggression or alarm alone.
calls.comments: Croak-rumble is listed by de Silva 2010 but was rare and not recognized by earlier wild studies as a separate call. Agreement is weak outside the primary inventory.

calls.acoustic_description: A rare combination call with a brief chirp-like leading segment followed by a lower-frequency rumble-like segment. The leading segment is short and tonal, and the second segment is lower in frequency and longer. Acoustic features: multi component, high frequency, tonal, short, low frequency, harmonic.
calls.semantic_description: Observed in bouts by adult females among companions, with young animals approaching the caller on two documented occasions. The available context suggests close social contact or attention involving companions and calves.
calls.comments: Chirp-rumble was observed only rarely in de Silva 2010 and is not independently recognized as a separate wild call type by McKay 1973 or Nair et al. 2009. Agreement is weak.

calls.acoustic_description: A rare male call with a brief softly audible first component around the low hundreds of hertz followed by a lower-frequency segment near the infrasonic range. Calls occur in long bouts separated by intervals of several seconds to tens of seconds, and the second segment may sometimes be absent. Acoustic features: multi component, low frequency, tonal, short, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males in musth during prolonged contests with other musth males and during courtship or guarding of an estrous female. It is associated with male reproductive competition rather than ordinary group contact.
calls.comments: de Silva 2010 documents this rare call from three wild musth males and treats it as possibly unique, but it had not previously been documented in wild or captive Elephas. Agreement is weak because evidence comes from one study and few events.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Wegdell et al. 2025 provide the most comprehensive recent inventory of the wild adult bonobo repertoire, quantitatively validating 11 acoustically distinguishable call types via random-forest analysis of >1500 calls from 53 individuals. It is explicitly framed as an updated repertoire and supersedes earlier qualitative descriptions (Bermejo & Omedes 1999; de Waal 1988), which used partially incompatible call categories. The 11 calls described here correspond one-to-one with the 11 call types in Wegdell et al. 2025.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, high-frequency tonal call, often with an inverted-U contour and sometimes with a short noisy onset. In the updated adult repertoire it also absorbs several bark-like variants that overlap acoustically with high hoots. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, noisy, short, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a conspicuous contact or attention-getting call, especially over distance, helping advertise the caller's presence or location and support cohesion between parties. Bark-like variants can also occur in food and arousal contexts, so function is broader than simple distance contact.
calls.comments: Wegdell et al. 2025 quantitatively validate high hoots, and Hohmann and Fruth 1994 describe high hoots as bonobo distance calls. The label is strong, though Wegdell et al. merge several previously named bark categories into high hoots while earlier studies split or named these calls differently.

calls.acoustic_description: A relatively long, high-frequency broadband call with variable noise and a flatter contour than high hoots, lacking a clear inverted-U shape at the beginning or end. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in high-arousal negative social situations, especially aggression, conflict, distress, or alarm-like episodes. It is best treated as an affectively intense call rather than a context-specific referential signal.
calls.comments: Screams are recognized in the older qualitative repertoires of de Waal 1988 and Bermejo and Omedes 1999 and are quantitatively retained by Wegdell et al. 2025. The label is strong, though detailed boundaries between screams and scream-like bark variants remain partly graded.

calls.acoustic_description: A very short, low-frequency, noisy call with an unshaped or weakly structured contour. It may be tonal or atonal and can sound breathy. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given during varied close-range activities such as grooming, resting, moving, and feeding. Recent semantic analysis suggests it can draw attention to the caller's ongoing activity, and food studies show that grunts can participate in food-associated sequences.
calls.comments: Grunts are retained as an acoustically discriminable adult call type by Wegdell et al. 2025 and are included among food-associated calls by Clay and Zuberbuhler 2009. The label is strong, though very soft, short-range calls are hard to sample in wild forest conditions.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, tonal, medium- to high-frequency call with a mostly flat contour, few harmonics, and low noise. It may include a small frequency squiggle or slight upward slope. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short.
calls.semantic_description: A highly flexible call used across feeding, travel, rest, aggression, alarm, nesting, grooming, and other daily contexts. Depending on context it can work as a mild coordination proposal or attention signal, with pragmatic context contributing strongly to interpretation.
calls.comments: Peeps are recognized across Bermejo and Omedes 1999, Clay and Zuberbuhler 2009, Clay et al. 2015, Berthet et al. 2025, and Wegdell et al. 2025. Multiple independent studies agree that peeps are a central bonobo call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, medium-frequency, noisy and atonal call with an unshaped spectrographic structure and high noise. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short.
calls.semantic_description: Associated primarily with play or positive social arousal, especially in close-range affiliative interactions. Published evidence is thinner than for peeps or contest hoots, so the semantic description should be treated as provisional.
calls.comments: Laughter appears in older qualitative repertoire work and is retained as an acoustically discriminable call type in Wegdell et al. 2025. The label is strong for call-type existence, though fewer studies focus specifically on laughter than on peeps, high hoots, or contest hoots.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency call with an unshaped contour, variable tonality, and relatively high noise. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with high-arousal situations and social coordination, including night-nest construction in recent semantic analysis. Its exact function remains broad and context-dependent.
calls.comments: Low hoots are retained by Wegdell et al. 2025 and appear in earlier repertoire descriptions. The label is strong, though hoot terminology has been split differently across studies.

calls.acoustic_description: A relatively long, tonal call with a low but high-pitched frequency range, usually flat or containing small frequency squiggles, and little noise. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used in spatial coordination and cohesion, especially to keep group members together. It can combine with peeps in socially sensitive contexts, where interpretation depends on the surrounding interaction.
calls.comments: Whistles are recognized in qualitative repertoire work and retained by Wegdell et al. 2025 as an acoustically discriminable adult call type. The label is strong, though functional treatment is less extensive than for peeps.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency tonal hoot with an inverted-U contour and low noise. In extended bouts it can be part of a multi-phase sequence with introductory, escalation, and let-down phases. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced especially by adult and subadult males as a socially directed challenge that can provoke a reaction such as chase, and can also occur in friendly play. It appears to assert social status or signal an intention to interact with socially important partners.
calls.comments: Contest hoots are described in de Waal 1988 and studied directly by Genty et al. 2014, and Wegdell et al. 2025 validates them acoustically in wild adult calls. The label is strong, though Bermejo and Omedes 1999 did not separate contest hoots from other hoots.

calls.acoustic_description: A very short, tonal call with an upward slope, medium noise, and relatively high frequency range compared with other low, short calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, noisy, short.
calls.semantic_description: A subordination or greeting-related signal in some bonobo populations, especially from lower-ranking individuals toward higher-ranking recipients. Its use varies sharply by population and social system.
calls.comments: Wegdell et al. 2025 validates pant grunts acoustically, and Schamberg et al. 2023 confirms regular production at LuiKotale. The label is medium because Schamberg et al. also report absence in adult bonobos at Kokolopori and summarize contradictory reports across populations.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency tonal call with a downward-pointing slope and low noise. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short.
calls.semantic_description: Used in social coordination and food-associated calling. Recent semantic analysis interprets yelps as stronger imperatives associated with changes in audience behavior, while food studies show yelps more often in sequences linked to less-preferred foods.
calls.comments: Yelps are recognized by Clay and Zuberbuhler 2009 and retained by Wegdell et al. 2025, and Berthet et al. 2025 includes yelps in the semantic/compositional analysis. The label is strong, though yelps and peep-yelps have partly overlapping meanings and acoustic space.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency tonal call with a variable contour, often an inverted-U or upward-pointing shape, and low noise. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in coordination contexts including group encounters, night-nest building, and travel between parties. In food contexts it appears in graded sequences, often with intermediate or broader food associations than pure peeps or yelps.
calls.comments: Peep yelps are recognized in food-call work, semantic/compositional work, and the 2025 quantitative repertoire. The label is strong, though peep yelps are acoustically and semantically close to both peeps and yelps in several analyses.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Stueckler et al. 2019 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is a peer-reviewed, species-specific wild study of the prolonged courtship that distinguishes advertisement calls from courtship calls and illustrates the courtship call. I found no formal whole-repertoire monograph for all life stages. Territorial and agonistic studies repeatedly use the male advertisement call as the acoustic signal that attracts females and repels rivals, so I treat "territorial call" as an alternate name for the advertisement call rather than as a separate call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, repeated bout call made of discrete tonal notes with upward frequency sweeps. Many French Guiana studies use a four-note call with note energy roughly in the 2.9-3.9 kHz range and calls repeated in bouts; playback stimuli based on natural recordings specify four notes of about 32-66 ms each, separated by tens of milliseconds, while geographic surveys report population differences including one-, three-, four-, and six-note arrangements. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, repetitive, multi component, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males from elevated structures on the forest floor during the breeding season. The call advertises territory occupancy, attracts female mating partners, elicits male phonotaxis and antiphonal calling in playback experiments, and contributes to territorial defense when combined with appropriate visual cues from an intruding male.
calls.comments: Stueckler et al. 2019, Narins et al. 2003 and 2005, Hoedl et al. 2004, Ringler et al. 2017, Rodriguez et al. 2020, and Peignier et al. 2022 all treat the male advertisement call as the prominent long-distance vocal signal of Allobates femoralis. Some papers call the same signal a territorial call in male-male contexts, but the call type itself is stable.

calls.acoustic_description: A lower-frequency, close-range buzzing call distinct from the advertisement call. Published descriptions characterize it as a broadband burst of pulses lasting about 0.5-1 s with dominant energy around 2.5-2.7 kHz; spectrograms show dense amplitude modulation across the call. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, pulsed, long, repetitive, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males after a female is nearby or in sight during the courtship sequence. Calling accompanies the courtship march in which the male leads the female through his territory toward oviposition sites; when the female stops following, the male returns and resumes courtship calling until she follows again.
calls.comments: Montanarin et al. 2011 and Stueckler et al. 2019 independently describe courtship calls in wild Allobates femoralis courtships, and Peignier et al. 2022 summarizes the same two-call distinction while measuring advertisement and courtship calls. The call type is therefore well supported despite fewer acoustic studies than the advertisement call.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Ouattara et al. 2009 in PLoS One is used as the primary_inventory spine because it explicitly enumerates the six loud call types consistently produced by free-ranging adult male Campbell's monkeys in Tai National Park and provides spectrographic illustrations, acoustic measures, field contexts, and predator-simulation evidence for those calls. This file keeps those six male loud calls as the primary inventory and adds only separately named wild female alarm/contact call types from Ouattara et al. 2009 and Coye et al. 2018, while excluding captivity-only female alarm variants.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-pitched loud call produced with the vocal sac, with little or no frequency modulation. Booms are acoustically inflexible, typically given as pairs, and often precede strings of other loud calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, loud, long, repetitive, tonal.
calls.semantic_description: Used in nonpredatory contexts, including cohesion or travel, falling trees or branches, disputes with neighboring groups, and unusual vocal excitement within the group. When placed before alarm-call sequences, booms reduce the predator specificity of the following calls in receiver responses.
calls.comments: Ouattara et al. 2009 PLoS One lists boom as one of six adult male loud calls, Ouattara et al. 2009 PNAS incorporates booms into context-specific male sequences, and Zuberbuhler 2002 experimentally tests boom-introduced sequences. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A single loud tonal utterance with a short duration and a descending main frequency band, starting around the low kilohertz range. Quantitative analyses support a recognizable krak stem, while also showing graded variation within male predator-alarm calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, loud, tonal, short, frequency modulated, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced after detecting leopards and other major terrestrial-predator evidence. Playback work shows receivers treat unsuffixed krak calls as more specific and urgent than krak-oo calls.
calls.comments: Krak is a primary adult male loud call in Ouattara et al. 2009 PLoS One, a sequence unit in Ouattara et al. 2009 PNAS, a tested leopard-alarm class in Zuberbuhler 2001, and part of the larger quantitative alarm-call analysis by Keenan et al. 2013. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A krak-like descending tonal stem followed rapidly by an acoustically stable oo suffix. The suffix creates a multi-component call, and later quantitative work treats suffixed forms as modifications of core male alarm stems with graded internal variation. Acoustic features: high frequency, loud, tonal, short, frequency modulated, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a general alert call to a wide range of disturbances rather than only leopard encounters. Receiver experiments show that the suffix reduces the specific leopard-alarm interpretation of the krak stem.
calls.comments: Krak-oo is one of the six primary adult male loud calls in Ouattara et al. 2009 PLoS One, appears as a sequence unit in Ouattara et al. 2009 PNAS, and is central to the suffixation playback study by Coye et al. 2015. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: In adult males, a short single tonal utterance with little frequency modulation and a main band around the low kilohertz range. Female alarm work also recognizes hoks as a basic wild alarm-call type, although fewer female hok recordings are available than female RRA calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, loud, tonal, short, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: In adult males, given mainly to crowned eagles and eagle-related evidence. In adult females, hoks are one of three basic alarm calls produced in response to disturbing or potentially dangerous events, but they were recorded much less often than RRA calls.
calls.comments: Hok is a primary adult male loud call in Ouattara et al. 2009 PLoS One, a predator-alarm class in Zuberbuhler 2001, and one of the three basic female alarm calls in Ouattara et al. 2009. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A hok-like, flat tonal stem followed by the acoustically stable oo suffix. The call is multi-component and belongs to the suffixed male loud-call set, with quantitative work indicating graded overlap among suffixed alarm-call forms. Acoustic features: low frequency, loud, tonal, short, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced to general canopy disturbances, including perched eagles, neighboring groups, conspecific opponents, and other arboreal events. It is often associated with threat posture or aggressive motivation rather than only predator detection.
calls.comments: Hok-oo is one of the six primary adult male loud calls in Ouattara et al. 2009 PLoS One and appears in the context-specific sequence analysis of Ouattara et al. 2009 PNAS. Zuberbuhler 2002 additionally supports boom-alarm sequence use involving Campbell's male alarm calls. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A suffixed loud tonal call with a wak stem whose main frequency band rises through the low kilohertz range, followed by an obligatory oo suffix. In females, wak-oos are also recognized as a basic alarm-call type, but wild female recordings are rare relative to RRA calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, loud, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: In adult males, associated with canopy disturbances such as eagles, other flying animals, and Diana monkey eagle alarms, but not reported for neighboring male contexts. In adult females, wak-oos are one of the basic alarm calls to potentially dangerous events.
calls.comments: Wak-oo is part of the six-call adult male primary inventory in Ouattara et al. 2009 PLoS One, appears in Ouattara et al. 2009 PNAS sequences, and is independently listed among the three basic female alarm calls by Ouattara et al. 2009. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A variable trill-like alarm call made from repeated and rapidly ascending pulses. Wild recordings separate several RRA variants that differ systematically in temporal and frequency-domain features. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, repetitive, pulsed, graded, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by females during predatory and nonpredatory disturbances. Variant structure is context-linked, and one captive human-response variant reported elsewhere was absent from the wild population and is not included here as a repertoire call.
calls.comments: Ouattara et al. 2009 identifies RRA trill calls as the dominant female alarm-call type in wild Campbell's monkeys, and Coye et al. 2018 includes RRA alarm calls among the common female calls analyzed in free-ranging groups. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-pitched harmonic contact call produced as a single simple unit, without the added high-pitched arched component found in combined harmonic contact calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, short, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Used by adult females as a contact call. In wild groups, simple calls were used mainly when predation risk was high, consistent with maintaining contact while limiting conspicuous identity-rich signalling.
calls.comments: Coye et al. 2018 analyzes SH calls in wild adult females and contrasts them with combined harmonic calls, but the female social-call repertoire is less comprehensively inventoried than the male loud-call system. Existence agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A combined contact call in which the low-pitched harmonic contact unit is merged with a high-pitched arched unit. Front and back combined forms are reported, depending on the relative position of the added arched unit. Acoustic features: low frequency, high frequency, tonal, harmonic, multi component, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Used by adult females when identity information is especially relevant, including mixed-species associations and socially important vocal exchanges. Combined calls are more identity-rich and easier to detect than simple calls, with a trade-off against eavesdropping risk.
calls.comments: Coye et al. 2018 analyzes CHf and CHb calls from wild adult females and treats them as common combined contact forms, but the evidence base is concentrated in one main study. Existence agreement is medium.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Smith 1972 is the primary inventory spine because it is a species-specific field-and-sonagram monograph whose vocal-display chapter explicitly recognizes 20 Carolina chickadee vocal displays. This repertoire includes those 20 displays as in-primary-inventory calls. Later peer-reviewed papers are used to update acoustic and semantic evidence for the chick-a-dee complex, song, tseet, and gargle-aligned calls, but no outside-inventory calls are added.

calls.acoustic_description: A rapid series of short high notes followed by a longer clear slink element; the clear elements are flattened or chevron-shaped and may be repeated two to eight times. Smith described variable pitch and occasional faint very high terminal notes, with intergrades toward rasp-bearing forms. Acoustic features: multi component, tonal, high frequency, frequency modulated, repetitive, short.
calls.semantic_description: Used in mild threat, patrolling, territorial disputes, close pair or flock encounters, predator-directed mobbing, precopulatory approaches, and adult responses to persistent fledgling begging. Smith interpreted the display as attack readiness inhibited by competing tendencies, often functioning as alerting or mild threat.
calls.comments: Smith treats T-slink as one of the 20 primary vocal displays, and Hailman later recognized Smith's T-slink/gargle-aligned material in the parid comparative framework. The label is not widely retained in recent experimental work, so agreement is medium rather than strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A stuttering introductory series of short notes followed by a noisy rasp with rapidly oscillating frequency. Smith described tee-rasp and slink-rasp variants as intergrading forms; Hailman treated these Smith calls as the Carolina chickadee material most comparable to the parid gargle. Acoustic features: multi component, noisy, broadband, pulsed, frequency modulated, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Given mainly in patrol, disputes, and close confrontations with other chickadees. Smith interpreted it as more strongly attack-biased than T-slink, while Hailman's comparative treatment places it with agonistic parid gargle displays.
calls.comments: Smith listed Click-rasp as a primary display, Hailman independently aligned the same Smith material with the parid gargle complex, and later Carolina chickadee summaries retain gargle as a major call category.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud robin-like chip with a harmonic chevron form, often produced in short series of about three to six notes. Smith noted frequent association with High See and occasional association with Loud Tee during movement into tense situations. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, loud, abrupt, short, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Heard in interflock disputes, patrolling toward dispute sites, dominant male patrols, male or pair disputes, and predator mobbing. Smith interpreted Chip as a strong threat signal reflecting conflict between attack and escape tendencies.
calls.comments: Smith clearly lists and illustrates Chip as a primary display, but later Carolina chickadee papers usually subsume related material into broader chick-a-dee or alarm categories.

calls.acoustic_description: A clear whistled song built from alternating higher and lower pitched tonal notes, typically starting high and commonly rendered as fee-bee-fee-bay. Smith described high notes and lower notes in regular alternation; later work treats this as one of the major Carolina chickadee vocal categories. Acoustic features: tonal, high frequency, frequency modulated, long, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced chiefly by males during spring patrolling, dawn singing, countersinging, and nesting contexts. Smith interpreted song as readiness for agonistic and pair-bond-limited behavior, and later sources emphasize its territorial and breeding-season display role.
calls.comments: Song is a primary Smith display and is repeatedly retained as a major Carolina chickadee vocal category in later acoustic and behavioral papers.

calls.acoustic_description: A song-like display in which the normal high-low alternation is imperfect, rearranged, or absent; Smith described patterns such as repeated high notes, repeated low notes, or high notes that slide upward rather than remaining flat. Acoustic features: tonal, high frequency, frequency modulated, graded, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used in the same broad patrolling and countersinging settings as Song, but Smith interpreted Song Variant as song motivation partly thwarted by lack of normal opportunity or social conditions.
calls.comments: Song Variant is explicitly one of Smith's 20 displays, but later sources generally discuss song variation without preserving this separate inventory category.

calls.acoustic_description: A quieter, usually shorter song-like display with clear tonal notes and sometimes a slight quaver. Smith often found it near Lisping Tee sequences and distinguished it from loud territorial Song by amplitude and social context. Acoustic features: quiet, tonal, high frequency, frequency modulated, short.
calls.semantic_description: Given mainly by birds moving near mates, nests, or young, including male approaches to females and family-group situations. Smith interpreted it as readiness for association and other pair-bond-limited behavior.
calls.comments: Faint Song is a primary Smith display, but later work usually groups quiet song-like sounds with song variation rather than maintaining this label.

calls.acoustic_description: A quiet song-like variant with the reduced amplitude of Faint Song but irregular or incomplete high-low organization. Smith treated it as the quiet counterpart of Song Variant. Acoustic features: quiet, tonal, high frequency, graded, short.
calls.semantic_description: Occurs in association-oriented breeding and family situations. Smith interpreted it as Faint Song motivation modified or thwarted by immediate social conditions.
calls.comments: It is included in Smith's primary inventory, but there is little independent literature retaining Faint Song Variant as a named category.

calls.acoustic_description: A rapidly repeated series of high chevron-shaped see notes, often with peaks above 8 kHz and waves of rising and falling frequency or amplitude. Smith reported that it almost always terminates in T-slink and can grade toward other high see-like calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Occurs in breeding-related interactions, including males near nesting females, dawn calling, copulation approaches, aggressive encounters, and patrol. Smith interpreted it as conflict among agonistic, escape, and pair-bond-limited tendencies.
calls.comments: Variable See is a Smith primary display, but later work rarely preserves it as a separate named call rather than discussing high see-like notes more broadly.

calls.acoustic_description: Similar to Dee in frequency, harmonic structure, and overall quality, but with irregular frequency fluctuations and notes that may subdivide into short chevrons. Smith described louder, longer, or higher forms during feeding approaches by adults to begging young. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, graded, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by nestlings, fledglings, and adult females begging from mates; also heard during adult feeding approaches to young. Smith interpreted it as readiness for bond-limited behavior, especially feeding, guarding, or copulation-related interactions.
calls.comments: Broken Dee is one of Smith's primary displays, and begging/dee-like calls are behaviorally plausible in parids, but later Carolina chickadee work rarely treats this exact label independently.

calls.acoustic_description: A series of chevron-shaped notes with emphasized, relatively long descending arms, typically in pairs, triplets, or short runs around the upper vocal range. Smith described a distinctive lisping quality and frequent occurrence before Faint Song. Acoustic features: tonal, high frequency, frequency modulated, repetitive, short.
calls.semantic_description: Used when birds associate closely, fly between mates or flock members, approach nests, and coordinate family movements. Smith interpreted it as balancing association with locomotory activity.
calls.comments: Lisping Tee is clearly included in Smith's primary inventory, but later literature does not commonly use the same named category.

calls.acoustic_description: A quiet series of narrow rounded dee-like chevrons with resonance harmonics, usually well spaced and often following Lisping Tee. Smith noted that it can intergrade with louder Dee forms. Acoustic features: quiet, tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Heard infrequently during close association, feeding-station encounters, and spring interactions near nests or females. Smith suggested an association-oriented function but treated the interpretation as tentative.
calls.comments: Soft Dee is a primary Smith display, but sparse later use of the label limits independent support.

calls.acoustic_description: A high, clear see note, usually a broad or flattened chevron in the upper frequency range, longer than High Tee and often given in series. Smith described intergradation with High Tee and longer squeal-like calls; later chick-a-dee work identifies high-frequency A-type notes as important in predator-related call variation. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, long, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with perched vigilance, observer or predator presence, hawks overhead, mobbing, feeding-station alertness, and disputes. Smith interpreted High See as an escape-biased alarm or attention signal, while later predator-context studies show high-frequency introductory note changes in chick-a-dee calls.
calls.comments: Smith lists High See as a primary display, and later chick-a-dee note-type studies independently support a high-frequency introductory note category with predator-related variation.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, clear high chevron note that can occur alone or as an introductory element in chick-a-dee sequences. Smith described intergradation with High See and Loud Tee; later note-type studies place comparable introductory notes in the combinatorial A/B/C/D chick-a-dee system. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, short, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Given during flight, alighting, perch changes, feeding-station activity, and tense social or predator-related situations. In modern chick-a-dee research, introductory high notes help modulate call meaning in predator and social contexts.
calls.comments: Smith includes High Tee in the primary inventory, and later studies independently identify high introductory note types within Carolina chickadee chick-a-dee calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A narrow chevron-shaped note with a pointed peak and multiple resonance harmonics, commonly occurring after High Tee-like notes and before Dee notes in chick-a-dee sequences. Smith described a mushy quality and intergradation with neighboring chick-a-dee elements. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, short, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in chick-a-dee combinations during movement, feeding, disputes, and tense or retreating situations. Smith interpreted it as intermediate between High Tee and Dee; later work shows that chick-a-dee note composition carries information about social and predator contexts.
calls.comments: Smith includes Chick as a primary display, and later work independently confirms chick-like note classes in the Carolina chickadee chick-a-dee call.

calls.acoustic_description: A series of broad, relatively flat chevron notes with stacked harmonics, commonly forming the terminal dee portion of chick-a-dee calls. Smith described series of several Dee notes and many prefixes by High See, High Tee, Chick, or combinations; later studies quantify the A/B/C/D syntax of these calls. Acoustic features: harmonic, tonal, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in feeding, flock coordination, disputes, predator contexts, and other tense associations. Playback and context studies show that chick-a-dee note composition affects receiver behavior, predator-threat coding, and food recruitment, making the Dee-bearing call complex a major combinatorial signal.
calls.comments: Smith lists Dee as a primary display, and later Carolina chickadee research repeatedly treats the chick-a-dee call and its D-note/dee component as a central, experimentally supported call complex.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, emphatic, skewed chevron note with a strong ascending arm and two or more resonance harmonics, usually produced in well-spaced short series. Smith described occurrence with High See, High Tee, and chick-a-dee combinations. Acoustic features: loud, tonal, harmonic, high frequency, abrupt, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Used across foraging, feeder visits, patrolling, nest guarding, hawk encounters, and disputes, but less often in direct face-to-face standoffs. Smith interpreted it as a sudden or high-level escape-biased warning signal.
calls.comments: Loud Tee is included in Smith's primary inventory, but later Carolina chickadee papers do not commonly retain this exact display label.

calls.acoustic_description: A very brief, high-pitched chevron note, usually single or well spaced and not used as a prefix to chick-a-dee sequences. Smith described variable fine shape and peaks in the upper frequency range; later work recognizes tseet as one of the commonly produced Carolina chickadee vocalizations. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, short, quiet, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Common in feeding, foraging, patrolling interruptions, nest trips, close approaches, and novel or mildly disturbing situations. Smith interpreted it as a weak escape-biased signal, while later summaries treat it as a common contact or coordination call.
calls.comments: Tseet is a Smith primary display and later Carolina chickadee work independently treats tseet as a common vocalization.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, high, elongated chevron-like call with a long descending arm; Smith described series that drop in frequency and grade toward harsher Scream forms. Acoustic features: loud, high frequency, frequency modulated, long, graded, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Heard from birds restrained in mist nets, traps, or the hand. Smith interpreted Squeal as thwarted escape and noted that it can attract attention from nearby chickadees and other species.
calls.comments: Squeal is a primary Smith display and fits widespread avian distress-call contexts, but later Carolina chickadee papers rarely treat it as a separate experimental category.

calls.acoustic_description: A harsh, loud distress call that grades from elongated Squeals into noisier broadband forms and intergrades completely with Hiss. Smith emphasized its rougher structure compared with Squeal. Acoustic features: loud, noisy, broadband, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by restrained birds in nets, traps, or the hand. Smith interpreted Scream as reflecting both thwarted escape and attack, and noted that it may draw mobbing or investigative responses from nearby birds.
calls.comments: Scream is listed in Smith's inventory, but its boundary with Squeal and Hiss is graded and later Carolina chickadee work rarely separates it.

calls.acoustic_description: A nearly formless, broadband, white-noise-like hiss that intergrades with harsh Screams. Smith treated Hiss as the noisiest end of the restraint-related distress series. Acoustic features: noisy, broadband, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given by restrained birds and interpreted by Smith as a display of thwarted escape combined with attack tendency. Its context suggests acute distress and defensive threat.
calls.comments: Hiss is a Smith primary display, but the category is closely graded with Scream and is not commonly isolated in later studies.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 is used as the spine because it explicitly enumerates the wild mature chimpanzee repertoire into 12 single units in Table 2 and analyzes how those units combine across the Tai repertoire. The full pant-hoot is treated here as a multi-unit sequence rather than a separate primary-inventory unit.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency noisy call with variable fundamental-frequency shape. It is usually produced singly or in short close-range bouts and grades toward bark-like calls in some recordings. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in close-range social and feeding contexts, including arrival at food and interactions where callers may retain, recruit, or coordinate with nearby partners. Food-associated rough grunts are best treated as an important contextual variant of the broader grunt unit.
calls.comments: Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 lists grunts as one of the 12 primary single units, and Fedurek and Slocombe 2013 plus Bouchard and Zuberbuhler 2022 independently study food-associated grunt use in wild chimpanzees. The label is strong, while rough/food grunts are treated as contextual variants rather than a separate inventory call.

calls.acoustic_description: A panted series of low-frequency noisy grunt elements, with voiced inhalations or panting inserted between short grunt pulses. Bouts are repetitive and can vary in amplitude and noisiness. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during close approaches and reunions, especially by lower-ranking individuals toward higher-ranking recipients. It functions as a directed greeting and submissive or appeasing signal in socially risky encounters.
calls.comments: Panted grunts are a primary inventory unit in Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 and are treated as a distinct greeting call by Laporte and Zuberbuhler 2010, Fedurek et al. 2021, and Desai et al. 2022. Agreement is strong despite variation in greeting sequence order.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency, highly tonal call with a mostly flat contour. Quiet variants are low-amplitude, while alarm-related variants can be longer, louder, and more frequency-modulated. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used across quiet coordination contexts such as resting and travel, and in alert or alarm contexts when callers encounter ambiguous or ambush-like threats. Receivers can use context and call variant to guide cautious approach, avoidance, or group coordination.
calls.comments: Hoos are retained as a primary inventory unit by Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022, while Crockford et al. 2018 and Schel et al. 2013 validate context-linked quiet and alarm variants. The broad hoo category is stable even though variants are split differently across studies.

calls.acoustic_description: A repetitive panted series of tonal hoo elements, with short pant intervals between units. It often follows single hoos and precedes climax elements such as panted barks or panted screams in pant-hoot sequences. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, long, repetitive, pulsed, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a central build-up component in long-distance pant-hoot sequences, which advertise caller presence, coordinate parties, and support spacing or inter-party contact. It can also occur in broader call combinations rather than only in canonical pant-hoots.
calls.comments: Panted hoo is listed as a primary unit in Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 and corresponds to the build-up phase described in pant-hoot studies such as Fedurek et al. 2017 and Clark and Wrangham 1993. The full pant-hoot sequence is not duplicated as a separate inventory unit.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, abrupt, noisy bark-like call with a relatively high fundamental frequency and dome-shaped contour when visible. It can grade acoustically toward grunts or screams, and context-specific bark variants differ in fine structure. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in high-arousal alarm or agonistic contexts, including encounters with snakes, hunting, and aggressive interactions. It can recruit others or signal readiness to retaliate, and in snake contexts it can combine with alarm hoos to produce a stronger recruitment effect.
calls.comments: Bark is a primary inventory unit in Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022, and Crockford and Boesch 2003, Schel et al. 2013, and Fedurek et al. 2015 all describe bark or waa-bark variants in wild chimpanzees. The label is strong, though some studies split context-specific barks.

calls.acoustic_description: A panted series of bark elements, each separated by short pant intervals. It shares the noisy dome-shaped bark structure but occurs as a repeated panted unit, often in climax positions of pant-hoot-like sequences. Acoustic features: high frequency, noisy, long, repetitive, pulsed, multi component, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a high-arousal panted unit in pant-hoot and other call combinations, often after hoos or panted hoos. Its meaning is best interpreted through sequence context, where it contributes to display, arousal, and social coordination.
calls.comments: Panted bark is listed as a primary inventory unit by Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 and corresponds to one climax option in pant-hoot sequence descriptions such as Fedurek et al. 2017. Agreement is strong for the unit's existence.

calls.acoustic_description: A noisy panted unit with low fundamental frequency when visible and a flat contour when measurable. It consists of short breathy pant elements and can appear alone or as the let-down part of longer sequences. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, repetitive, pulsed.
calls.semantic_description: Occurs as an independent panted unit and as a let-down component in pant-hoot-like sequences. Recent event-based work links pants especially with approach, affiliative, and play-related events, while pant-hoot literature treats them as part of long-distance display sequences.
calls.comments: Pant is one of the 12 primary units in Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 and is also recognized as a let-down element in pant-hoot sequence descriptions such as Fedurek et al. 2017. The label is strong for inventory inclusion.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, high-frequency, noisy and broadband call with a relatively flat midsection. Screams can occur singly or in repeated bouts, and acoustic structure varies with caller role and interaction severity. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during agonistic interactions, especially by victims of aggression. The calls can recruit or influence bystanders and convey information about the severity of aggression and the caller's social situation.
calls.comments: Scream is a primary unit in Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 and is recognized as a core wild chimpanzee call in Slocombe and Zuberbuhler 2007 and Fedurek et al. 2015. The label is strong even though subtypes vary with caller role and event severity.

calls.acoustic_description: A repeated panted series of high-frequency noisy scream elements separated by short pant intervals. It shares the broadband scream profile but occurs as a panted multi-element unit, often in climax positions of pant-hoot-like sequences. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, long, repetitive, pulsed, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a high-arousal panted unit in long-distance or socially intense sequences, including pant-hoot climaxes and other call combinations. It likely contributes arousal, display, or recruitment value depending on the surrounding unit sequence.
calls.comments: Panted scream is a primary inventory unit in Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 and is one of the recognized pant-hoot climax options in Fedurek et al. 2017. The label is strong for existence, although panted and non-panted scream semantics are often discussed together.

calls.acoustic_description: A short noisy mechanically produced sound unit, including lip smacks and raspberries, without measurable fundamental frequency or tonal contour in the primary inventory. Acoustic features: noisy, short, repetitive, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Included in the inventory as a single unit that can occur alone or in combinations. Recent event-based analysis links non-vocal sounds especially with close-range affiliative events such as grooming, rather than long-distance contact.
calls.comments: Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022 includes non-vocal sounds as one of the 12 units in the primary inventory, but this category is mechanically produced rather than strictly vocal and is less often treated as a classic chimpanzee call type. The inventory rule supports inclusion, while the label remains medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, highly tonal call with a mostly flat contour and a fundamental frequency around the mid-to-high range of the chimpanzee repertoire. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, short, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: A relatively rare call in the adult wild repertoire. It is treated in recent whole-repertoire work as a single unit in combinations, with context suggesting close-range social or low-intensity distress and attention-related use rather than loud long-distance signaling.
calls.comments: Whimper is listed as a primary inventory unit by Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022, with 78 occurrences, but it has much less independent call-specific literature than grunts, hoos, barks, or screams. The existence label is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A rare noisy panted roar unit with low-frequency energy and spectral bands below the visible fundamental frequency. It occurs as a panted form, especially as a possible let-down component in pant-hoot-like sequences. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, long, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Best supported as a rare let-down or terminal component of long-distance display and contact sequences. Its specific standalone function remains uncertain because the primary inventory recorded it only rarely.
calls.comments: Panted roar is included in the primary inventory of Girard-Buttoz et al. 2022, but it occurred only once there and is mainly known as a pant-hoot let-down option in sequence descriptions. The label is weak because the inventory support is sparse.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Luis et al. 2021 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it compares wild recordings from nine Atlantic and Mediterranean common bottlenose dolphin populations and identifies a shared acoustic repertoire organized into whistles, burst-pulsed sounds, bray-series elements, and bangs, with 24 signal subtypes. This file conservatively represents the broad wild-supported classes and the best-supported named call types rather than every regional subtype. Signature whistle and echolocation click train are retained as outside-spine entries because they are central, independently supported Tursiops truncatus sound types, while several regional or weakly contextualized labels such as chirps and low-frequency narrow-band sounds are left out.

calls.acoustic_description: A narrow-band tonal whistle type whose individually distinctive information is carried mainly by the frequency-modulation contour rather than by voice quality. It is often produced in repeated loops or bouts, with start, end, minimum, and maximum frequencies varying among individuals and populations. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used by individuals to broadcast their own identity and in matching or copying exchanges that address a particular social partner. It is especially associated with maintaining or re-establishing social contact among familiar individuals in a fission-fusion society.
calls.comments: Janik and Sayigh 2013 review five decades of signature-whistle research, Kriesell et al. 2014 identifies signature whistles in a wild Namibian population, Janik 2000 reports matching by wild Scottish dolphins, and King and Janik 2013 uses playback with wild dolphins. The named call type is strongly supported even though Luis et al. 2021 grouped whistles by contour rather than by signature status.

calls.acoustic_description: A narrow-band tonal signal with a continuous frequency-modulated contour. Wild populations show multiple contour shapes, including sinusoidal, convex, concave, upsweep, downsweep, and constant-frequency forms; measured frequency ranges commonly span several kilohertz into the ultrasonic edge of common recording bandwidths. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during social interaction, group cohesion, coordination, and changes in group composition or behavior. Some whistles carry individual identity, while the wider whistle class includes shared or non-signature contours whose specific meanings remain less resolved.
calls.comments: Whistles are a primary Luis et al. 2021 category recorded across all nine wild populations and are also described in the Walvis Bay inventory by Gridley et al. 2015 and in the Jones et al. 2020 review. The broad whistle class is uncontested, even though sources split contours and signature status differently.
