calls.acoustic_description: A broadband pulsed signal made of rapidly repeated pulses with short inter-pulse intervals, commonly high enough that the pulses are perceived as a fused sound rather than separate clicks. Wild recordings show graded variation in pulse rate, duration, and spectral concentration, with several named subtypes separated by time-frequency structure. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, pulsed, repetitive, short, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in a range of high-arousal social and foraging contexts, including agonistic encounters, displays, coordinated activity, and feeding-related events. The class is contextually broad, and several named subtypes have more specific regional or behavioral associations.
calls.comments: Burst-pulsed sounds are a primary Luis et al. 2021 repertoire category, are quantitatively analyzed in wild Sado estuary dolphins by Luis et al. 2016, are included in the Walvis Bay inventory by Gridley et al. 2015, and are synthesized by Jones et al. 2020. The broad class is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A multi-unit rhythmic sequence with repeated bray elements, often lower in frequency than whistles and organized into bouts. Studies separate multiple element or sequence variants, and transition probabilities among elements can be nonrandom. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, pulsed, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with feeding in several wild populations, including salmonid feeding in the Moray Firth and foraging-related bray-series contexts in later repertoire studies. Some populations or studies also link bray-series use to social or aggressive contexts, so the context is not restricted to one prey type.
calls.comments: Janik 2000 documented food-related bray calls in wild Scottish dolphins, Luis et al. 2021 includes bray-series elements across the multi-population inventory, and Luis et al. 2019 plus Pace et al. 2022 analyze bray sequence structure in Portugal and the Mediterranean. The call type is strongly supported, although local variants differ.

calls.acoustic_description: A short broadband pulsed subtype with rapid pulse repetition and noisy spectral structure. It is separated from other pulsed signals by quantitative time-frequency features in wild recordings, but grades toward neighboring burst-pulse subtypes. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, pulsed, repetitive, short, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Most often reported within feeding-associated pulsed sequences in wild multi-population analyses. It can occur in temporal proximity to other foraging-related pulsed elements, so its independent contextual role remains only partly resolved.
calls.comments: Squawk appears as a named pulsed subtype in Luis et al. 2016 and as one of the signal subtypes shared across all nine populations in Luis et al. 2021, with Jones et al. 2020 reviewing the naming problem for pulsed dolphin sounds. Agreement is medium because squawks are well supported as a subtype but boundaries with other burst-pulsed sounds are graded.

calls.acoustic_description: A rapidly repeated broadband pulsed subtype with short inter-pulse intervals and a creaking temporal texture. Quantitative studies separate it from squawks, bangs, and variable-rate click trains, while retaining it inside the broader pulsed-sound continuum. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, pulsed, repetitive, short, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Reported in wild feeding-associated pulsed sequences and recorded across sampled populations. Its use is best understood as part of foraging-related acoustic sequences rather than as a stand-alone context with tested receiver meaning.
calls.comments: Creaks are named in Luis et al. 2016 and are one of the pulsed subtypes shared across all nine populations in Luis et al. 2021. Agreement is medium because the label is supported in modern wild-repertoire work but remains one of several closely related pulsed categories.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-energy, isolated broadband pulse with abrupt onset and short duration. It is treated separately from pulse trains and bray-series elements because its energy is concentrated in single, conspicuous pulse events rather than repeated units. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, pulsed, short, abrupt, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with prey detection or prey-startling during foraging in wild repertoire studies. Its possible role as an attention-getting or display sound remains less directly tested than its foraging association.
calls.comments: Bangs are a primary Luis et al. 2021 category recorded at all nine sites, with high-energy isolated pulses also treated in Luis et al. 2016 and reviewed by Jones et al. 2020. Agreement is medium because the label is modern and useful, but historical pulsed-sound nomenclature overlaps with related names.

calls.acoustic_description: A train of very short, high-frequency broadband clicks with variable inter-click intervals. Source-parameter measurements from free-ranging bottlenose dolphins report microsecond-scale click durations, high source levels, centroid frequencies from tens to over one hundred kilohertz, and strong directionality. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, pulsed, repetitive, short, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Used during object inspection, navigation, prey search, prey approach, and prey capture. During foraging, click timing changes as animals close on targets, and rapid buzz phases are associated with close-range prey-capture attempts.
calls.comments: Echolocation click trains are central to bottlenose dolphin bioacoustics, are described from wild foraging contexts by Nowacek 2005, quantified from free-ranging bottlenose dolphins by Wahlberg et al. 2011, and reviewed as a core Tursiops sound type by Jones et al. 2020. It is outside the Luis et al. 2021 spine because that inventory focused on selected vocal elements and treated only variable-rate click trains among its subtype set.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Bezerra and Souto 2008 is the first and standard inventory of the common marmoset vocal repertoire based on wild animals, enumerating approximately 13 call types (phee, trill, trillphee, twitter, chirp, tsik, ek/egg, ock, squeal, and others) with quantitative acoustic measurements and behavioural contexts from three groups in Atlantic Rain Forest. Agamaite et al. 2015 provides a larger quantitative classification (12 simple + 13 compound call types) but is based on captive animals; per our captivity rule it is treated as a complementary acoustic source rather than the spine. Bezerra and Souto remains the canonical wild repertoire for this species.

calls.acoustic_description: A long, narrowband tonal call, usually composed of one or more sustained pulses with gradual frequency modulation. Phee strings can repeat several phee units with short silent intervals between them. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, long, repetitive, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a long-distance contact call, especially when individuals are separated or visually occluded, and in antiphonal exchanges. The call carries information about caller identity and social group and can also participate in territorial spacing.
calls.comments: Phees are described in the wild repertoire by Bezerra and Souto 2008, are one of the four major quantitative call classes in Agamaite et al. 2015, and are the focus of antiphonal calling studies by Miller et al. 2010 and Miller and Thomas 2012. Agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A narrowband tonal call distinguished by a sinusoidal frequency-modulated contour, usually shorter-range and less sustained than phees. The fundamental frequency commonly lies in the upper kilohertz range and can vary with age. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used mostly at short range during social contact or vocal exchanges between nearby individuals. Wild work also shows age-related differences in trill pitch, indicating developmental variation in this common call.
calls.comments: Trills are recognized in the wild repertoire of Bezerra and Souto 2008, analyzed quantitatively by Agamaite et al. 2015, and examined in wild ontogenetic work by Bezerra et al. 2009. The call type is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A phrased, wideband call made from a sequence of regularly spaced upward frequency-modulated sweeps. Phrase number, inter-phrase interval, and sweep structure vary between callers and populations. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, frequency modulated, repetitive, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in social vocal exchanges among nearby individuals and often answered by another twitter or a different contact call. Its exact functional range is less well resolved than phee calls, but it is a common social-coordination vocalization.
calls.comments: Twitter calls are included in Bezerra and Souto 2008 and form one of the major call classes in the quantitative acoustic analysis by Agamaite et al. 2015. Agreement is strong for existence.

calls.acoustic_description: An extremely short, high-intensity broadband call with a rapid frequency sweep, often produced in repeated strings. It is among the broadest-band simple calls in quantitative analyses. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, frequency modulated, short, abrupt, loud, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during mobbing or alarm responses to threatening stimuli, including predator models, and can be repeated rapidly in high-arousal situations. Experimental studies also link tsik calling with coping or stress modulation during threats.
calls.comments: Tsik calls are described in wild common marmosets by Bezerra and Souto 2008 and treated as a simple call type by Agamaite et al. 2015. Clara et al. 2008 and Cross and Rogers 2006 further support the mobbing-call category experimentally.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, harsh broadband call that often appears near tsiks or as a component of mobbing-related compound calls. It is less acoustically elaborated than phees, trills, or twitters. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with alarm, mild anxiety, mobbing, or threat contexts, often in combination with tsiks and related short calls. Its independent function is less clearly tested than that of the phee or tsik.
calls.comments: Egg calls are included in the wild repertoire by Bezerra and Souto 2008 and identified as a simple call type by Agamaite et al. 2015. Existence is strong even though the functional literature is thinner.

calls.acoustic_description: A compound call beginning with a tsik-like element followed by one or more egg-like elements with very short silent intervals. It can occur within longer variable strings of tsik, egg, and related short calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, repetitive, multi component, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in mobbing or predator-related contexts as part of the short-call alarm system. It appears to package tsik and egg elements into a recurring compound form, but its meaning relative to single tsiks remains incompletely tested.
calls.comments: Agamaite et al. 2015 treats tsik-egg as a recurring compound call type, and Bezerra and Souto 2008 supports the wild short-call repertoire from which it is built. The label is medium because compound-call boundaries are less settled than simple calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A long narrowband tonal call that begins with a sinusoidal frequency-modulated trill portion and transitions into a sustained phee-like portion. It is acoustically intermediate between trills and phees and is one of the four most prevalent simple call classes in quantitative analyses. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used in contact and coordination contexts at intermediate ranges, often interchangeable with trills or phees in social exchanges. Together with twitter, phee, and trill it accounts for the great majority of social calls produced.
calls.comments: Trillphee is described in the wild repertoire of Bezerra and Souto 2008 and is one of the four most prevalent simple call types in Agamaite et al. 2015, accounting (together with twitter, phee, and trill) for ~81% of all calls collected. Independent recognition across wild and captive analyses is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A short tonal call with a brief frequency-modulated contour, shorter and more punctate than trills or phees. It is among the shorter simple calls in the marmoset repertoire and is frequently used as a sequence boundary marker. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, short, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in short-range social contexts and sequence transitions, particularly at the start and end of vocal exchanges. Sequencing analyses report that chirp calls have the highest probability of initiating and terminating call sequences.
calls.comments: Chirp is described as a wild call type by Bezerra and Souto 2008 and treated as a sequence-boundary unit in later sequencing analyses of common marmoset calls. The label is medium because chirp is not separately quantified in Agamaite et al. 2015 and may be partially absorbed into peep or short tonal categories in captive classifications.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-frequency, broadband and noisy call with much of its energy concentrated below 2 kHz, making detailed spectro-temporal measurement in the wild difficult. It is acoustically distinct from the higher-pitched tsik and egg short calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Used in mobbing and predator-defence contexts, often together with tsik and egg calls as part of the short-call alarm system. Behavioural descriptions treat ock as a low-pitched mobbing-related signal directed at terrestrial or near-ground threats.
calls.comments: Ock is described in the wild repertoire of Bezerra and Souto 2008 and retained as a simple call type by Agamaite et al. 2015. Both wild and captive sources recognize it as distinct from tsik and egg, supporting a strong existence label.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Conner 1985 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is a peer-reviewed field study of free-ranging Common Ravens that identified 18 call types from 1,210 tape-recorded vocalizations and linked many of them to behavior at roosts, nest sites, mountain ridges, and a landfill. This file includes the Conner call types with clear wild contextual support and omits rare or mainly unknown-context types. The well-studied food-associated haa, who, and chii calls are added outside the primary inventory because later wild field and playback studies treat them as named, context-specific call types.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-pitched, loud, harmonic call with variable pitch and duration; Conner measured many calls with fundamentals in the low hundreds of hertz and noted that some tokens ascended while others descended. The form grades broadly and includes individually and situationally variable versions. Acoustic features: low frequency, harmonic, loud, frequency modulated, graded, short.
calls.semantic_description: Given by single birds and small groups while soaring, arriving near roosts, assessing feeding sites, responding to nest disturbance, watching disputes nearby, and during object play by likely immature birds.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 identified Caw as the most frequent Virginia call type, and Brown 1974 reported very common Kaww-like calls in free-ranging Alaskan ravens. Agreement is medium because transliterations and boundaries vary across inventories.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, harsh, low-frequency sound with a pulsing growl-like quality. Conner illustrated several variants and treated them as a distinct harsh call type. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, broadband, pulsed, loud, short.
calls.semantic_description: Heard during close conflicts over roost position, especially when two birds were trying to occupy the same position in roost trees.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 recorded and illustrated the wild Virginia call and noted that growl-like calls were among the types shared with Gwinner's raven work. Agreement is medium because the independent support includes captive comparison, while the wild contextual basis is from Conner.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft harmonic call, sometimes monotonal and sometimes multiharmonic, with a whine-like spectral trace. Conner's examples show several variants within the same soft call family. Acoustic features: harmonic, tonal, quiet, frequency modulated, graded, short.
calls.semantic_description: Given at roosts during apparent agonistic confrontations over position, especially by individuals retreating from a dominant bird.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 identified Whine as a named wild call and compared whines with Gwinner's repertoire; Szipl et al. 2017 independently analysed defensive calls in wild ravens, but did not map them one-to-one onto Conner's Whine label.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, rapidly repeated, drum-like rattle. Conner compared its temporal texture to woodpecker drumming and illustrated it as a repeated broadband series. Acoustic features: pulsed, repetitive, broadband, noisy, loud, long.
calls.semantic_description: Given by paired birds during courtship at roosts, nest sites, and feeding areas, often with conspicuous body postures and most often during the breeding season.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 recorded Rattle as a named wild call type and noted rattle among call types shared with Gwinner's study. Agreement is medium because the clearest wild contextual support is from one detailed field inventory.

calls.acoustic_description: A shortened caw-like element, often followed by longer caws; Conner described it as about half the duration of ordinary caws and illustrated a sharp initial element with variable following notes. Acoustic features: abrupt, short, repetitive, harmonic, loud, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Given when birds were disturbed at nests, flushed from roosts, or reacting to predators or human, dog, vehicle, and raptor disturbances near roosts and feeding sites.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 clearly separated Staccato caw from Caw in wild recordings, but later raven studies usually discuss alert or defensive calls more broadly.

calls.acoustic_description: A sputter-like call usually given as rapid staccato couplets, with some series containing four to nine clucks in quick succession. Acoustic features: abrupt, pulsed, repetitive, broadband, short, noisy.
calls.semantic_description: Heard when nesting pairs were disturbed, during visits near young, and when birds were displaced from preferred roost positions.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 identified and illustrated Cluck as a wild call type with repeated observations. The label is not widely retained in later raven playback work.

calls.acoustic_description: A very loud, high-pitched honking call with many harmonics reaching high frequencies; Conner recorded it rarely but described it as the loudest call he heard. Acoustic features: high frequency, harmonic, loud, abrupt, short.
calls.semantic_description: Given during attacks on intruding ravens near nest cliffs, during chases at roosts, and during an agonistic encounter between paired birds at a feeding site.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 identified Kow in wild Virginia ravens, Brown 1974 reported common Koww-like Alaskan calls, and Conner noted comparison with Gwinner's material. Agreement is medium because spellings and exact boundaries vary.

calls.acoustic_description: A resonant tonal sound like a muted bell or xylophone note, sometimes given loudly over distance and sometimes softly with a hoot-like quality. Conner illustrated multiple variants. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, loud, quiet, long, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Given during aerial and ground courtship by paired birds, often with display postures, and also heard during a close male-male interaction.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 recorded Bell-like sounds in wild ravens and noted that bell-like calls were among those shared with Gwinner's ravens. The wild semantic base is still mostly one field study.

calls.acoustic_description: A harsh staccato couplet or triplet with repeated elements. Conner illustrated the call as a compact multi-element sequence. Acoustic features: abrupt, repetitive, noisy, multi component, short.
calls.semantic_description: Given while one raven chased another, especially in aggressive interactions around roosting or nesting areas.
calls.comments: Conner 1985 lists Ku-uk-kuk as a wild Virginia call, and Brown 1974 reports stereotyped multisyllabic Kukuk-like calls in Alaskan ravens. Naming varies, so agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A far-reaching long yell transcribed as haa. Analyses of marked wild birds show individually distinctive variation in fundamental-frequency and intensity-related parameters, with a highly harmonic structure and measurable variation in duration, harmonicity, jitter, amplitude modulation, and frequency contour. Acoustic features: loud, long, harmonic, frequency modulated, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when ravens encounter rich food that is defended, monopolized, difficult to access, or otherwise risky; receivers are attracted to the caller or speaker, and playback studies show that responses depend on caller identity, familiarity, sex, and rank.
calls.comments: Heinrich and Marzluff 1991, Bugnyar et al. 2001, Boeckle et al. 2012, Szipl et al. 2015, and Boeckle et al. 2018 all treat haa/yell as a named raven food-associated call. It is outside Conner's primary inventory but strongly supported in later wild and playback work.

calls.acoustic_description: A short yell transcribed as who and distinguished from the longer haa and juvenile chii calls in studies of raven food-associated calls. Acoustic features: short, loud, harmonic, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Given by dominant ravens when landing at feeding sites or during the feeding situation; unlike haa calling, its occurrence is tied to the caller's behavior near food rather than to prior visual access to inaccessible food.
calls.comments: Bugnyar et al. 2001 and Szipl et al. 2015 identify who as one of the raven food-associated calls, with Boeckle et al. 2018 noting it as a dominant-male-associated food call. It has less direct acoustic analysis than haa.

calls.acoustic_description: A long juvenile yell transcribed as chii and treated as the juvenile form of the food-associated call complex, with developmental links to juvenile begging-like vocal behavior. Acoustic features: long, loud, harmonic, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by juvenile ravens in food contexts; its use changes as young birds become independent, and later studies interpret it as linked to hunger, age class, and juvenile status near feeding sites.
calls.comments: Bugnyar et al. 2001 and Szipl et al. 2015 identify chii as the juvenile long yell, and Boeckle et al. 2018 discusses juvenile food-associated calls as age-linked. Support is good but narrower than for haa.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Coye et al. 2022 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it explicitly compiles long-term published wild data on Diana monkey vocal units, call combinations, contextual use, and call rates, and summarizes the adult female repertoire as eight non-combined calls and eight combined calls. This file includes those 16 female call types and supplements them with the three well-supported adult male long-distance call variants separated by Zuberbuhler et al. 1997. Captivity-only calls are not included.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, multi-syllable long-distance call made as a sequence of discrete syllables. In the 1997 analysis, non-predation long-distance calls had a median of about seven syllables and were acoustically distinguishable from the shorter leopard-alarm variant. Acoustic features: loud, long, repetitive, multi component, low frequency.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by resident adult males in non-predation contexts such as spontaneous calling, neighboring male calls, and loud environmental disturbances. It is treated as a long-range signal involved in intergroup spacing and male advertisement.
calls.comments: Zuberbuhler et al. 1997 separates non-predation long-distance calls from leopard and eagle variants, and Coye et al. 2022 treats male Diana monkey calls as a distinct sex-specific repertoire component. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud long-distance alarm variant composed of discrete syllables, typically with fewer syllables than eagle-alarm sequences. Zuberbuhler et al. 1997 reports a median of about three syllables per call in leopard contexts, with acoustic parameters separating it from the eagle variant. Acoustic features: loud, long, repetitive, multi component, low frequency.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males in response to leopards or leopard vocalizations. Calling is often paired with predator approach and functions in warning conspecifics and advertising detection to ambush predators.
calls.comments: The male leopard alarm is identified by Zuberbuhler et al. 1997, reanalyzed across populations by Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2008 and 2016, and used in later coordination playbacks by Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2016. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud long-distance alarm variant made from repeated syllables. In Zuberbuhler et al. 1997, eagle-context calls contained more syllables than leopard-context calls, with a median of about eight syllables, and differed from leopard calls across several measured acoustic parameters. Acoustic features: loud, long, repetitive, multi component, high frequency.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males in response to crowned eagle calls or eagle encounters. Receivers respond as if an aerial predator is present, and males may approach the source during anti-predator signaling.
calls.comments: The male eagle alarm is a central call type in Zuberbuhler et al. 1997, Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2008, Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2016, and Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2016 Current Biology. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, repetitive vocal unit described in the comparative repertoire as the Diana monkey counterpart of short repetitive threat structures in Campbell's monkeys. The label reflects a pulsed, rough-sounding sequence rather than an arched tonal contour. Acoustic features: repetitive, pulsed, noisy, broadband, short.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult females during threatening or socially negative events. It is treated as a threat-related unit rather than a contact or relaxed-social call.
calls.comments: Coye et al. 2022 lists Brrr as one of eight adult female Diana monkey non-combined calls, but there are fewer dedicated studies of Brrr than of arched contact calls and predator alarms. Existence agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A short repetitive unit, distinct from the arched A-family calls and from the trill-based H and L units. It can occur alone or as the first unit in combinations with arched calls. Acoustic features: repetitive, short, abrupt, noisy.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with socially negative or potentially dangerous events. In combinations, it contributes event information that listeners distinguish from the L unit.
calls.comments: R is listed by Candiotti et al. 2012, experimentally manipulated by Coye et al. 2016, and included in the Coye et al. 2022 repertoire synthesis. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-pitched, trill-based unit. It can occur alone or precede a full or broken arched A unit in two-unit combinations. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with neutral social or external contexts and often used as the first unit in contact combinations that help maintain group cohesion and convey caller-related information.
calls.comments: L is one of the named vocal structures in Candiotti et al. 2012, one of the experimentally manipulated event units in Coye et al. 2016, and one of the eight non-combined calls in Coye et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-pitched, trill-based unit. It is acoustically separated from the lower-pitched L unit and from the arched A-family calls, and can occur alone or before Af or Ab. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with socially positive or relaxed contexts. In combinations, it contributes positive or relaxed contextual information before the identity-bearing arched unit.
calls.comments: H is one of the four female vocal structures reported by Candiotti et al. 2012 and one of the eight non-combined calls in Coye et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A full arched tonal contour with a rising and falling frequency pattern. It is the full-arch member of the A-family contact calls and carries individual acoustic variation in its frequency contour. Acoustic features: tonal, frequency modulated, long, high frequency.
calls.semantic_description: Used by adult females to maintain spatial and social cohesion, especially when caller identity is important. It can occur alone or after H, L, or R.
calls.comments: Af is the common contact or clear call analyzed by Uster and Zuberbuhler 2001 and Candiotti et al. 2012 Biology Letters, used in the Candiotti et al. 2012 combination study, experimentally manipulated by Coye et al. 2016, and listed by Coye et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A broken-arch member of the A-family, lacking the complete full-arch contour of Af. It can occur alone or as the arched unit in H-Ab, L-Ab, and R-Ab combinations. Acoustic features: tonal, frequency modulated, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in the contact-call system of adult females, with the arched unit contributing caller-related information during group coordination and social spacing.
calls.comments: Ab is included in Candiotti et al. 2012 and listed by Coye et al. 2022 as one of the eight non-combined female calls and as a component in several combinations. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: An arched call variant with lower frequencies truncated and a sharper upper contour than Af. It can occur as a single call or after R in R-Alk combinations. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, abrupt, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used by adult females in alarm contexts, particularly as one of the Diana-specific arched alarm units described for the female repertoire.
calls.comments: Alk is identified by Coye et al. 2022 as one of the Diana-specific female units, and Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2014 supports female predator-specific alarm-call production. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A multi-component arched unit consisting of a short high-pitched arched note followed by an Alk-like truncated arch. It can occur alone or after R in R-W combinations. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, short, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Used by adult females in alarm contexts as one of the Diana-specific arched alarm units.
calls.comments: W is listed by Coye et al. 2022 as one of two Diana-specific arched alarm units, and Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2014 supports female predator-specific alarm categories. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit combination beginning with the low-pitched L trill and ending with the full arched Af unit. The final arched contour is the main frequency-modulated element. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used as a contact combination in neutral contexts, with the first unit contributing contextual information and the full arch contributing caller identity.
calls.comments: L-Af is listed in Candiotti et al. 2012 and Coye et al. 2022, and L/A combinations were experimentally tested by Coye et al. 2016. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit combination beginning with L and ending with the broken arched Ab unit. It shares the low-pitched introductory component with L-Af but has an incomplete arched ending. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used in neutral contact contexts as part of the adult female combination system, with an introductory contextual unit followed by an identity-bearing arched unit.
calls.comments: L-Ab is included in the Candiotti et al. 2012 combination set and in the Coye et al. 2022 repertoire synthesis. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit combination beginning with the high-pitched H trill and ending with the full arched Af unit. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in socially positive or relaxed contexts, combining contextual information from H with caller-related information from Af.
calls.comments: H-Af is reported by Candiotti et al. 2012 and included among the eight Diana monkey combined calls in Coye et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit combination beginning with H and ending with the broken arched Ab unit. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in socially positive or relaxed contexts as part of the adult female combination system.
calls.comments: H-Ab is included in both Candiotti et al. 2012 and the Coye et al. 2022 synthesis of female Diana monkey combinations. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit combination beginning with the short R unit and ending with the full arched Af unit. Acoustic features: repetitive, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used in socially negative or potentially dangerous contexts, while also conveying caller-related information through the Af unit. Playback tests show receivers attend to both the event unit and the arched unit.
calls.comments: R-Af is reported by Candiotti et al. 2012, used in Coye et al. 2016 playback work, and included by Coye et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit combination beginning with R and ending with the broken arched Ab unit. Acoustic features: repetitive, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Used in socially negative or potentially dangerous contexts as part of the adult female combination system.
calls.comments: R-Ab appears in Candiotti et al. 2012 and in the Coye et al. 2022 list of Diana monkey female combinations. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit alarm combination beginning with the short R unit and ending with the truncated arched Alk unit. Acoustic features: repetitive, high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Used in alarm contexts by adult females. Coye et al. 2022 treats R-Alk as a Diana monkey alarm combination generated by combining R with an arched alarm unit.
calls.comments: R-Alk is included in the Coye et al. 2022 female combination inventory, and Stephan and Zuberbuhler 2014 and 2016 support the broader female predator-specific alarm system. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A two-unit alarm combination beginning with R and ending with the multi-component W arched unit. Acoustic features: repetitive, high frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Used in alarm contexts by adult females as one of the Diana monkey combinations that pairs R with a species-specific arched alarm unit.
calls.comments: R-W is listed in Coye et al. 2022 as one of the eight female Diana monkey combined calls, and later alarm studies support female predator-specific alarm production. Existence agreement is strong.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Prat et al. 2016 is used as the spine because it explicitly enumerates the five distinct Egyptian fruit bat vocalization types shown in its repertoire figure--mating calls, isolation calls, seclusion/distress calls, echolocation clicks, and aggression calls--and states that continuous recording covered the complete repertoire used during the 2.5 month experiment. Prat et al. 2017 supports this inventory with the larger annotated vocalization dataset.

calls.acoustic_description: A variable sequence of broad-band, multi-harmonic syllables, usually arranged as one to about twenty syllables per vocalization. Syllable-level feature distributions overlap among feeding, mating-protest, perch, and sleep contexts, but their spectral structure carries classifier-detectable information about caller, addressee, context, and likely interaction outcome. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, harmonic, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced as directed pairwise protest or squabble calls in the roost, especially during conflicts over food, mating attempts, perch proximity, and positions in the sleeping cluster. It is the most common social call class in the primary inventory and is often addressed to a specific interaction partner.
calls.comments: Prat et al. 2016 lists aggression calls as the most common Egyptian fruit bat call type, Prat et al. 2017 archives the annotated vocal corpus, and Prat, Azoulay et al. 2017 uses agonistic vocalizations as playback material. The label is medium rather than strong because the main evidence comes from the same research tradition and because aggression subcontexts are graded rather than sharply separate call types.

calls.acoustic_description: A male social vocalization produced in bouts during mating interactions. The primary inventory illustrates it as a lower-frequency harmonic call sequence, mostly within the frequency range plotted below about 15 kHz, but call-specific acoustic measurements are limited. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males during mating interactions. In the annotated repertoire it is separated from aggression calls, pup isolation calls, adult seclusion/distress calls, and echolocation clicks by caller class and mating context.
calls.comments: Prat et al. 2016 explicitly lists male mating calls in the primary inventory, and Prat et al. 2017 documents the broader annotated recordings across contexts. The label is medium because the call is clearly named in the repertoire spine but has little independent call-focused treatment.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-fundamental-frequency pup call often emitted in trains. Herbert 1983 describes calls built from one to seven frequency-modulated units with up to three harmonics, usually upward-then-downward sweeps; call duration is mainly about 110-180 ms, and the first harmonic decreases with age from roughly 21-25 kHz at day 5 to 14-18 kHz by day 69. Later ontogeny studies show these calls developing toward adult-like social vocalizations. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, harmonic, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by newborn and young pups when isolated from, left by, or detached from the mother in the roost. In separation trials the call attracted maternal searching and contact, and it declines as the young become independent.
calls.comments: Isolation calls are independently documented by Herbert 1983 and by the Prat et al. 2015, 2016, and 2017 ontogeny and repertoire studies. The call is consistently treated as a pup call rather than an adult social-call variant.

calls.acoustic_description: A repeated adult social vocalization illustrated as a distinct broad-band, multi-harmonic call class. It shares the general broad-band structure of other Egyptian fruit bat social calls, but the available literature provides little call-specific acoustic quantification beyond the repertoire example and annotated dataset. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, harmonic, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Emitted mostly by distressed adults that are separated from others. The call is associated with social seclusion rather than with a specific resource conflict, mating interaction, pup separation, or sonar use.
calls.comments: Prat et al. 2016 lists seclusion/distress calls as a primary repertoire class, and Prat et al. 2017 provides the annotated database supporting the context labels. The label is medium because independent call-focused confirmation is limited.

calls.acoustic_description: A hyper-short, low-energy, broad-band impulse signal produced by rapid tongue movement and emitted in repeated, often paired click trains. Adult clicks are brief and low in energy but matched to the species' hearing sensitivity, and newborn pups already produce paired hyper-short clicks and can steer the sonar beam. Acoustic features: broadband, short, abrupt, quiet, repetitive, pulsed.
calls.semantic_description: Used for non-social acoustic orientation, obstacle avoidance, and movement through dark or cluttered spaces. It is included as a repertoire element because the primary inventory lists it, but its function is sonar rather than social signaling.
calls.comments: Holland et al. 2004 directly measures R. aegyptiacus echolocation clicks, Prat et al. 2016 lists echolocation clicks in the primary repertoire, and Smarsh et al. 2021 documents click production from birth. The existence of lingual echolocation clicks in this species is strongly established.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Gustison et al. 2012 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the main wild comparative inventory that identifies gelada homologous and derived call types and ties the derived calls to field-observed social contexts. The file emphasizes call types with independent wild support in later acoustic, playback, sequence, contact-call, and mating studies, and does not import the older zoo-only adult repertoire as standalone entries when wild evidence is lacking.

calls.acoustic_description: A short exhaled call with measurable fundamental-frequency and formant structure. In male affiliative sequences it averaged about 0.3 s and formed the short-duration end of the graded grunt-to-moan continuum; female contact grunts also vary acoustically by individual and behavioral state. Acoustic features: low frequency, short, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in close-range affiliative, foraging, travelling, and socializing contexts. Female contact-grunt similarity is structured at the band level, consistent with a role in maintaining cohesion in the multilevel society, while males also use grunts in affiliative sequences directed to females.
calls.comments: Exhaled grunts are part of the Gustison et al. 2012 wild inventory, are one of the six units in the Gustison et al. 2016 sequence analysis, are measured spectro-temporally by Gustison and Bergman 2017, and are the focus of Painter et al. 2024 female contact-call analyses.

calls.acoustic_description: A short ingressive grunt. In wild male sequences it is typically slightly shorter than the exhaled grunt, and it has mean fundamental and formant values similar to exhaled grunts while differing in production direction. Acoustic features: low frequency, short, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by both males and females in close-range affiliative sequences. In males it is commonly combined with exhaled grunts and more elaborate derived calls during approaches, grooming-related interactions, and post-conflict affiliative exchanges with females.
calls.comments: Inhaled grunts are identified in Gustison et al. 2012, appear as a discrete unit in the 4,747-call Gustison et al. 2016 sequence data, and are spectro-temporally measured by Gustison and Bergman 2017.

calls.acoustic_description: An elongated exhaled grunt-like call on the long-duration side of the grunt-to-moan continuum. In male sequence analyses, exhaled moans are substantially longer than exhaled grunts and can last several seconds. Acoustic features: low frequency, long, frequency modulated, tonal, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by adult males in close-range affiliative sequences directed toward females, including approaches, grooming-related interactions, and periods after female-female conflicts. Playback work shows that female receivers attend more to male sequences containing derived calls than to grunt-only sequences.
calls.comments: Exhaled moans are a derived gelada call in Gustison et al. 2012, are one of the six labeled sequence units in Gustison et al. 2016, and are used in the derived-call playback design of Gustison and Bergman 2016.

calls.acoustic_description: A long ingressive moan that forms the extended-duration counterpart to the inhaled grunt. Sequence analyses distinguish it from inhaled grunts by duration, and acoustic comparisons show a relatively low mean fundamental frequency and first formant. Acoustic features: low frequency, long, frequency modulated, tonal, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by adult males as part of close-range affiliative vocal sequences with females. It contributes to the complexity of male sequences used during approaches, grooming-related interactions, and other bonding contexts.
calls.comments: Inhaled moans are identified in Gustison et al. 2012 and then treated as a separate labeled unit in the Gustison et al. 2016 wild sequence corpus and the Gustison and Bergman 2017 acoustic comparison.

calls.acoustic_description: A cyclic, strongly modulated call produced with rhythmic oral movements. It contains repeated amplitude and spectral pulses, often around speech-like rates, and shows larger formant bandwidths than exhaled grunts. Acoustic features: frequency modulated, repetitive, pulsed, multi component, graded, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by adult males in close-range affiliative vocal sequences directed toward females. Playback studies using sequences with wobbles show that females orient to and remain near derived-call sequences more than grunt-only sequences.
calls.comments: Wobbles are derived gelada calls in Gustison et al. 2012, were analyzed as speech-like vocalized lip-smacking by Bergman 2013, and are included in Gustison et al. 2016 and Gustison and Bergman 2017 acoustic datasets.

calls.acoustic_description: A conspicuous vocalized yawn with relatively high fundamental and first-formant frequencies and broad modulation across formants. It is longer than grunts and has one of the widest spectral profiles among the measured male derived calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, loud, long, broadband, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by adult males in affiliative vocal sequences with females, where it contributes to sequence elaboration. Later playback work in a zoo colony also supports the acoustic salience of yawn sounds, but the wild production context comes from the field sequence and derived-call studies.
calls.comments: Vocalized yawns are a derived gelada call in Gustison et al. 2012, one of the six wild male sequence units in Gustison et al. 2016, and a measured call type in Gustison and Bergman 2017. Pedruzzi et al. 2024 further validates audible yawn vocalizations experimentally in a zoo colony.

calls.acoustic_description: A female call produced in sequences before genital contact. Wild copulation recordings classify it from spectrograms and fundamental-frequency contours, with sequence length varying across mating events. Acoustic features: repetitive, tonal, frequency modulated, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by females while approaching a leader male before copulation. Longer sequences are associated with longer copulations and a higher likelihood of the end-copulation call, consistent with soliciting and sustaining successful mating.
calls.comments: Gustison et al. 2012 reports the pre-copulation call, and Zanoli et al. 2022 analyzes it in 187 wild copulations. It is well supported contextually, though less independently studied than the core affiliative sequence units.

calls.acoustic_description: A call type produced in sequences during copulation and classified from spectrograms and fundamental-frequency contours. Male and female call sequences can overlap during the copulatory event. Acoustic features: repetitive, frequency modulated, tonal, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during copulation, with males typically calling from the beginning to the end and females sometimes calling concurrently. The calls participate in multimodal sexual communication with gaze and other mating signals.
calls.comments: Gustison et al. 2012 reports male gelada copulation calls in the wild repertoire, and Zanoli et al. 2022 quantifies male and female copulation-call production during wild mating events.

calls.acoustic_description: A single female call type identified at the final stage of copulation. In wild recordings it was acoustically distinct from other female mating vocalizations in f0-based random-forest classification and was cross-checked against video-visible mouth opening. Acoustic features: tonal, frequency modulated, short.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by females at the end of copulation and not recorded outside copulatory contexts in the field sample. It is interpreted as a marker of copulation completion and is associated with the outcome of the mating sequence.
calls.comments: Zanoli et al. 2022 identifies this as a new female vocal type from wild copulation recordings and reports strong classification performance for the class, but it currently rests mainly on one dedicated study.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Schassburger 1993 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the dedicated monograph on timber-wolf vocal communication and enumerates 11 major call classes: howl, whine, whimper, yelp, growl, snarl, woof, bark, moan, whine-moan, and growl-moan. Harrington and Asa 2003 review those classes as a graded repertoire with some weakly replicated boundaries, so every Schassburger major class is included here and the moan complex is marked with weak agreement where appropriate. Squeak is added as an outside-inventory call because later peer-reviewed work treats it as acoustically and contextually distinct rather than only a whistle-whimper variant.

calls.acoustic_description: A long, loud, mostly tonal harmonic vocalization with a low to mid fundamental frequency and slow frequency modulation. Solo howls range from flat to breaking contours, while chorus howls contain overlapping individual howls and may incorporate short bark-howl or howl-bark components. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, loud, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used for long-distance contact, pack assembly, spacing among packs, territorial advertisement, and social bonding. Field playback and elicitation studies show that response probability varies with pack location, pups, food resources, relationship quality, and other social or ecological factors, and acoustic analyses support individual and pack identity cues.
calls.comments: Howl is a major Schassburger 1993 class and is independently treated as a core wolf call by Harrington and Asa 2003, Theberge and Falls 1967, Harrington and Mech 1979, Zaccaroni et al. 2012, and Sadhukhan et al. 2019. Authors split or name howl variants differently, but the call type itself is uncontested.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-pitched harmonic call with a relatively pure tonal structure, usually soft and frequency modulated. It is longer and less abrupt than a yelp or squeak, but it grades into whimper and moan-like variants in some descriptions. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, short, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given at close range during appeasement, greeting, care solicitation, social contact, and frustrated or distressed motivation. Pup and adult accounts associate whines with social dependence or reduced aggression rather than threat displays.
calls.comments: Whine is a Schassburger 1993 major class and is retained by Harrington and Asa 2003, Coscia et al. 1991, Passilongo et al. 2017, and Sadhukhan et al. 2019. Agreement is medium because whines, whimpers, squeaks, and whine-moans form a graded high-frequency family that some studies merge and others split.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, soft, high-pitched harmonic call with a clear tonal trace and frequency modulation. It is typically shorter than a whine and less abrupt than a yelp, and Schassburger's whistle-whimper subtype overlaps with later squeak terminology. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, short, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used at close range in friendly greeting, appeasement, contact with familiar pack members, and pup-adult interactions. It generally accompanies social approach or nonaggressive motivation.
calls.comments: Whimper is a Schassburger 1993 major class and appears in Harrington and Asa 2003, Passilongo et al. 2017, Sadhukhan et al. 2019, and Weir et al. 2022. Agreement is medium because later authors sometimes reserve whimper for one subtype and sometimes use squeak or social squeak for neighboring acoustic forms.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, abrupt, high-pitched harmonic call, often more intense and steeper in contour than a whimper or whine. It may occur singly or in short series and grades toward squeak-like calls at lower intensity. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, short, abrupt, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during sudden close-range distress, pain, fear, rough contact, or intense social interaction. In pups it can solicit adult attention, while adult accounts associate it with submissive or conflict-related situations.
calls.comments: Yelp is a Schassburger 1993 major class and is also listed by Harrington and Asa 2003, Coscia et al. 1991, and Passilongo et al. 2017. Agreement is medium because yelps sit near whimpers and squeaks in the high-frequency graded continuum and are less often analyzed quantitatively than howls, barks, or growls.

calls.acoustic_description: A low, rough, broadband vocalization with noisy energy and variable duration. It can be sustained or pulsed, and it grades into bark-growl, growl-bark, snarl, and growl-moan forms as intensity and mouth posture change. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in close-range agonistic encounters, dominance displays, food defense, warnings, and tense interactions with pack members or outsiders. It signals aggressive or defensive motivation and often increases social distance.
calls.comments: Growl is a Schassburger 1993 major class and one of the broad classes retained by Harrington and Mech 1978 and Harrington and Asa 2003. Coscia et al. 1991, Passilongo et al. 2017, and Sadhukhan et al. 2019 also treat growls or growl-like calls as part of the wolf repertoire.

calls.acoustic_description: A rough, low-frequency, broadband aggressive sound closely allied to growling, typically more intense and often associated with exposed teeth or open-mouth threat displays. Acoustic boundaries with growl are graded rather than sharply discrete. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in close-range threats, dominance contests, food defense, and escalated social conflict. It functions as a high-intensity warning or aggressive display and may precede attack or withdrawal.
calls.comments: Snarl is a Schassburger 1993 major class and is reviewed by Harrington and Asa 2003; Passilongo et al. 2017 also lists snarls among aggressive wolf vocalizations. Agreement is medium because many accounts treat snarling as a growl-associated display rather than a fully independent acoustic class.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low, abrupt broadband sound that is softer and less explosive than a full bark. It has little sustained tonal structure and grades toward bark as amplitude and intensity increase. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced as a short-range warning or alert call, especially when an adult detects disturbance near pups or a den, and in other close-range defensive contexts. It can draw the attention of nearby pack members without the intensity of full barking.
calls.comments: Woof is a Schassburger 1993 major class and is retained by Harrington and Asa 2003, Coscia et al. 1991, and Passilongo et al. 2017. Agreement is medium because woofs are frequently described as low-intensity barks and the boundary between woof and bark is graded.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, explosive, low-pitched broadband call with abrupt onset and relatively high amplitude. Barks may occur singly or in repeated bouts and grade into woofs, bark-growls, and bark-howls when combined with neighboring call forms. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in immediate defensive or alarm situations, including disturbance at den or rendezvous sites, pup defense, food defense, and close-range confrontation with humans, other wolves, or other threats. It can recruit attention and warn nearby pack members.
calls.comments: Bark is a Schassburger 1993 major class and one of the broad wolf vocalization classes summarized by Harrington and Mech 1978 and Harrington and Asa 2003. Coscia et al. 1991, Passilongo et al. 2017, and Sadhukhan et al. 2019 add independent support for bark or bark-combination forms.

calls.acoustic_description: A relatively low, soft, sustained vocalization with more tonal structure than a growl and a lower frequency range than most whines. In Schassburger's scheme it is a central member of the moan complex and grades toward whine-moan and growl-moan forms. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Described mainly in close-range social situations with mixed appeasement, discomfort, or care-related motivation. Infant accounts report moan-like sounds in early development, while adult accounts treat moans as low-intensity social signals rather than long-distance calls.
calls.comments: Moan is included because it is one of Schassburger's 1993 primary-inventory classes and is reviewed by Harrington and Asa 2003, with infant support from Coscia et al. 1991. Agreement is weak because later reviews note sparse wild evidence and little independent quantitative replication of adult moan categories.

calls.acoustic_description: A graded intermediate call between whine and moan, with soft tonal or harmonic structure and a longer, lower contour than typical whimpers or squeaks. It may sound like a whine that falls into a lower moan-like component. Acoustic features: frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, quiet, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Associated with close-range social approach, appeasement, or ambivalent motivation in Schassburger's adult repertoire. It is best treated as a hypothesized intermediate social call rather than a strongly established standalone signal.
calls.comments: Whine-moan is retained because Schassburger 1993 lists it as a major class and Harrington and Asa 2003 reviews it, but independent peer-reviewed work rarely uses it as a discrete category. Agreement is weak because it is an intermediate point on a graded whine-to-moan continuum.

calls.acoustic_description: A low, graded intermediate between growl and moan, with some rough or noisy energy but a softer and more moan-like contour than a typical growl. It belongs to the low-frequency moan complex rather than to long-distance vocalizations. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, harmonic, long, quiet, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Described in close-range ambivalent or low-intensity agonistic social situations, where aggressive and appeasing motivations appear mixed. It is best interpreted as a weakly established graded variant of the growl-moan continuum.
calls.comments: Growl-moan is retained because it is a Schassburger 1993 primary-inventory class and appears in Harrington and Asa 2003, but independent studies generally discuss growls or moans rather than this mixed label. Existence agreement is weak because the category is graded and sparsely replicated.

calls.acoustic_description: A brief, high-frequency, tonal harmonic call with frequency modulation, often produced in short close-range bouts. It overlaps historically with Schassburger's whistle-whimper subtype, but recent studies separate squeaks or social squeaks from whines and whimpers. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, short, quiet, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in close-range affiliative social interactions, especially greeting and friendly contact among familiar animals. Individual acoustic differences reported for squeaks suggest that they can also carry caller identity information.
calls.comments: Squeak is outside the Schassburger 1993 major-class list, but Weir et al. 2022 treats squeaking as a distinct close-range affiliative vocalization, Sadhukhan et al. 2019 separates social squeak in Indian wolves, and Passilongo et al. 2017 identifies squeaks in wild chorus recordings. This is enough peer-reviewed support for inclusion.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Behr and von Helversen 2004 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the peer-reviewed inventory that classified daytime vocalizations of 16 wild male S. bilineata from Costa Rica by acoustic properties and social context, explicitly listing seven vocalization types--echolocation pulses, barks, chatter, whistles, screeches, territorial songs, and courtship songs. Because this spine is adult-male and day-roost focused, later peer-reviewed pup, female, and distress-call studies are retained as outside-inventory calls when they provide separate acoustic and behavioral evidence.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, stereotyped, multi-element male song composed of repeated syllable types such as short tonal elements, buzzes, trills, noise bursts, and echolocation-like calls. Long buzz syllables are harsh, loud, and low in fundamental frequency, and song elements can be rhythmically organized. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, noisy, harmonic, repetitive, multi component, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by territorial males at day roosts, especially around reoccupation and departure periods, to repel rivals, advertise territory-holder quality, and attract females. Playback work shows territorial males respond more strongly to lower-frequency songs, and field experiments show male song can attract dispersing females.
calls.comments: Behr and von Helversen 2004 separate territorial song from courtship song in wild Costa Rican males, Behr et al. 2006 analyzes territorial-song syllables and male quality, and Burchardt et al. 2019 uses territorial songs as one of three focal vocalization types. The call type is strongly established.

calls.acoustic_description: A long, complex male song produced in display bouts and built from variable elements, especially trills, noise bursts, short tonal calls, and quasi-constant-frequency calls. Trill parameters differ among males and can contribute to individual repertoires. Acoustic features: frequency modulated, tonal, noisy, harmonic, long, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males when displaying toward females, often as part of multimodal courtship that also includes wing-sac scent displays and hovering. It is associated with mate attraction, individual male display, and potential female choice.
calls.comments: Behr and von Helversen 2004 explicitly distinguishes courtship songs from territorial songs in wild male Saccopteryx bilineata, while Davidson and Wilkinson 2004 and Voigt et al. 2008 support the broader role of male acoustic display in this mating system.

calls.acoustic_description: A short male call resembling an echolocation pulse in frequency range and modulation, but typically longer and with the spectral maximum emphasized in the fundamental frequency. The inventory reports barks around 10 ms in duration, longer than the shorter echolocation pulses recorded in the same roost context. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by adult males at day roosts when no obvious interaction was underway, and sometimes during agonistic conflicts. The context suggests a low-intensity alert or mildly aggressive social signal rather than a song display.
calls.comments: Behr and von Helversen 2004 explicitly lists barks as one of seven daytime male vocalization types and separates them from echolocation pulses by duration and spectral emphasis. The label is medium because later work rarely treats bark as a focal call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A train of many brief calls, with sequences reaching up to several seconds and individual elements lasting only a few milliseconds. Single chatter elements resemble echolocation pulses but are usually more strongly modulated, and pauses within a train are regular enough to form a rhythmic sequence. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Frequently emitted by roosting adult males throughout the day without an obvious immediate interaction. Chatter can also be embedded with other vocalization types and can transition into trill-like sequences within courtship songs, linking it to low-arousal roost communication and male display structure.
calls.comments: Behr and von Helversen 2004 includes chatter in the seven-type primary inventory and describes it as a sequence distinct from isolated barks, echolocation pulses, and songs. Agreement is medium because subsequent studies mention it mainly as part of the broader repertoire rather than analyzing it independently.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, stereotyped tonal male call with an upward frequency-modulated stroke that often ends in a downward modulation. The first harmonic is typically the loudest, placing the main energy near the ultrasonic range characteristic of echolocation pulses, while part of the call remains audible to humans. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, long, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males during hover displays in front of females, synchronized with specialized wing strokes and scent-fanning behavior. Females often answer the hover display with screeches, and related Trinidad work links comparable screech-inverted-V male calls to female numbers in male territories.
calls.comments: Behr and von Helversen 2004 lists whistles as a distinct inventory type, and Davidson and Wilkinson 2004 analyzes comparable male screech-inverted-V vocalizations in the same mating system. Agreement is medium because terminology and syllable grouping differ between studies.

calls.acoustic_description: A broad-spectrum, noisy adult call with variable noisiness and sometimes discernible multiharmonic components. Screeches are typically longer than barks and echolocation pulses, and individual calls can include both noisy and multiharmonic sections. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, harmonic, short, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by both sexes during agonistic encounters, especially territorial conflicts. Female screeches are also common responses to male hover displays and often occur immediately before or alongside male whistles.
calls.comments: Behr and von Helversen 2004 identifies screeches as one of the seven inventory types and notes production by both sexes, while Davidson and Wilkinson 2004 reports screech-related responses in male call interactions. The label is medium because later studies use partly different composite-call terminology.

calls.acoustic_description: A complex multisyllabic call containing introductory or simple variable elements followed by composite and stereotyped elements. Pup calls commonly contain several element types in a repeated sequence and encode individual, group, and age-related information in different syllable portions. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, noisy, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by pups to elicit maternal care and support mother-pup reunions. Related isolation-call forms also occur later in life, including use by young or subordinate males in affiliative or appeasement contexts, so the adult semantic scope is broader than pup care alone.
calls.comments: Isolation calls are central in Knornschild and von Helversen 2008, Knornschild et al. 2012, Fernandez and Knornschild 2017, and Burchardt et al. 2019. These independent analyses of recognition, group signatures, ontogeny, and rhythm strongly agree that this is a discrete call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A pup-directed female call produced as a monosyllabic series, usually several short syllables in succession. Compared with adult-directed female calls, maternal directive calls differ in timbre and have lower peak frequency. Acoustic features: frequency modulated, tonal, short, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by mothers toward their own pups, especially in mother-pup communication during the pup's ontogeny and early flight or care-related interactions. It is a female pup-directed vocal feedback signal.
calls.comments: Fernandez and Knornschild 2020 directly analyzes maternal directive calls from wild colonies, and Knornschild and von Helversen 2008 provides the earlier mother-pup recognition framework. The label is medium because the named call type is well supported but detailed treatment is concentrated in one focused study.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, noisy, multi-syllable distress vocalization with several described categories; the most common playback stimulus category consists of buzz syllables with a tonal part. Spectrograms show broad-band energy and pulsed buzz structure. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, pulsed, repetitive, multi component, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced under extreme physical distress, such as capture-like predator contexts. Playback experiments show that conspecifics are attracted to distress calls within or near day roosts, consistent with threat assessment or mobbing.
calls.comments: Eckenweber and Knornschild 2016 analyzes distress calls, separates distress-call categories, and uses them in conspecific playback experiments with wild Saccopteryx bilineata. The call type is directly supported, but the label is medium because detailed S. bilineata evidence is concentrated in one focused primary study.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-frequency ultrasonic pulse emitted in sequences. Search sequences can be monotonous around a stable frequency or frequency-alternating with low-note and high-note calls, and release recordings show rhythmic trains of many short elements. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Used for orientation, navigation, and insect prey capture during flight, with frequency-alternating sequences associated with active foraging. Echolocation sequences can also contain sex-specific or individual information, so they may contribute to social communication beyond sonar.
calls.comments: Ratcliffe et al. 2011 directly records echolocation calls in Panama, Burchardt et al. 2019 analyzes echolocation call sequences from wild Costa Rican bats, and Behr and von Helversen 2004 includes echolocation pulses in the broader repertoire. The call type is uncontroversial.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Bohn et al. 2004 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it explicitly summarizes the vocal repertoire of P. hastatus as three commonly emitted vocalization types--group-specific foraging calls, low-amplitude echolocation calls, and infant isolation calls--and gives frequency ranges for each. It is not a standalone wild repertoire monograph, so the call entries are cross-supported by call-specific wild and field-playback studies for screech calls, by infant-call acoustic and discrimination studies for isolation calls, and by echolocation/foraging studies for sonar calls. No additional captivity-only call types are included.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, audible-frequency broadband call concentrated in the low-frequency range for this species, reported around 4-18 kHz in the group-distinctive analysis and summarized as about 6-11 kHz in the repertoire/hearing study. Calls have distinctive amplitude-frequency spectra and measurable spectral variables that separate social groups and cave colonies more clearly than individuals. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult females when leaving day roosts, during travel, and at feeding sites. Field observations and playback experiments in Trinidad support use in attracting social group mates, coordinating departures and foraging movements, and identifying group membership during access to patchy food resources.
calls.comments: Boughman 1997, Wilkinson and Boughman 1998, Boughman and Wilkinson 1998, Boughman 1998, and Bohn et al. 2004 all use the screech or group-specific foraging call as a named P. hastatus call type. The call type is strongly established even though the social-foraging context varies among populations.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-frequency, frequency-modulated pup call with harmonic energy, summarized for P. hastatus as spanning roughly 15-100 kHz. Detailed recordings show a typical double-note form with two short frequency-modulated notes separated by a brief interval; spectral shape is relatively stable during early development while duration decreases and peak frequency can increase with age. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, short, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by nonvolant pups when separated from or needing to be located by mothers in the roost. Females use these calls for offspring recognition, and discrimination experiments show that adult females can distinguish pup calls in a task relevant to maternal identification.
calls.comments: Bohn et al. 2004 lists infant isolation calls as one of the three common P. hastatus vocalization types, and Bohn et al. 2007 provides a dedicated acoustic and behavioral-discrimination study of those pup calls. The named call type is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-amplitude ultrasonic sonar pulse composed of short broadband frequency-modulated sweeps. Bohn et al. 2004 summarizes the species' echolocation calls as about 1-3 ms pulses sweeping from roughly 80 to 40 kHz, and hearing studies treat these signals as distinct from the lower-frequency screech calls and higher-peak-energy infant isolation calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, broadband, short, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during orientation and foraging. Field and experimental work supports use in locating fruit displayed away from foliage, and the calls are part of the species' normal sonar system for navigating and detecting targets in cluttered habitats.
calls.comments: Echolocation calls are listed as one of the three common P. hastatus vocalization types by Bohn et al. 2004, discussed in Koay et al. 2002 as part of the species' auditory ecology, and behaviorally linked to fruit detection by Kalko and Condon 1998. The type is strongly established.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Reichert and Hobel 2018 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it explicitly records and analyzes the two primary vocalization types in male Hyla cinerea, advertisement calls and aggressive calls. This is not a formal whole-life-stage repertoire monograph, but I found no stronger species-specific peer-reviewed inventory. General accounts mention release, warning, alarm, or rain calls, but I did not find peer-reviewed species-specific acoustic and semantic descriptions detailed enough to add them under the current inclusion rules.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, short, repeated, single-note harmonic call. Natural and synthetic-call studies describe a call about 120-160 ms long, repeated roughly once or twice per second in choruses, with a bimodal spectrum: a low-frequency peak near 0.9-1.1 kHz and higher energy near about 2.7-3.3 kHz. The call is not a pulse train, but its waveform has fine-temporal periodicity near 300 per second and a brief pulsatile onset. Acoustic features: low frequency, high frequency, tonal, harmonic, pulsed, short, repetitive, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males in breeding choruses at wetlands, ponds, and other calling sites. Female phonotaxis and mate-choice experiments show that females selectively approach species-typical advertisement calls, while field studies show that calling attendance is central to male mating opportunities and that the calls also attract eavesdropping satellite males.
calls.comments: Reichert and Hobel 2018 list advertisement calls as one of the two primary Hyla cinerea vocalization types, and Oldham and Gerhardt 1975, Gerhardt 1974, Gerhardt 1978, Gerhardt 1987, Gerhardt et al. 1987, Perrill et al. 1982, and Velez et al. 2012 all treat this male call as the core breeding signal. Terminology varies between advertisement, mating, and mate-attraction call, but the call type is stable.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, strongly amplitude-modulated call that is pulsed throughout rather than mainly at the onset. Recent playback stimuli based on population means model the Hyla cinerea aggressive call as about 125 ms long with five pulses and spectral components near 900 and 2700 Hz; comparative repertoire work measures it separately from the advertisement call using modulation depth, relative amplitude, duty cycle, pulse rate, and related timing traits. Acoustic features: low frequency, high frequency, tonal, harmonic, pulsed, short, repetitive, loud, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males during close-range male-male interactions in breeding aggregations and calling spaces.
