Field and playback studies distinguish responses to synthetic encounter/aggressive calls from responses to mating calls, consistent with a role in repelling or spacing rival males rather than attracting mates.
calls.comments: Reichert and Hobel 2018 list aggressive calls as the second primary Hyla cinerea vocalization type, Gerhardt 1978b reports that males produce two distinctive calls with rare acoustic intermediates, Perrill et al. 1982 uses synthetic encounter calls in field experiments, and Hobel and Rodriguez 2022 uses aggressive-call stimuli derived from population means. The encounter/aggressive naming differs, but the discrete call type is strongly supported.

taxonomy_basis.summary: No single published paper enumerates the Parus minor vocal repertoire as a whole. The literature on this species is dominated by Suzuki and colleagues' work on the alarm-call subsystem (jar calls, ABC notes, D notes, and ABC-D compositional sequences); reviews note that Japanese tits have "over 10 different notes" but no comprehensive inventory has been published. Broader repertoire knowledge is mostly extrapolated from the closely related great tit (Parus major), whose 40-note song-and-call system is documented separately. Every call in this file is therefore a literature-grounded addition rather than an inventory entry.

calls.acoustic_description: A repeated harsh call made of short noisy elements that are acoustically discrete from chicka calls. It is typically produced as a bout of jar-like notes rather than as an ordered A-B-C-D sequence. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, repetitive, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adults in nest-defence contexts especially when confronted with Japanese rat snakes. Playback of jar calls causes adult receivers to direct search toward the ground, and incubating females use conspecific alarm-call information to assess predation risk.
calls.comments: Suzuki 2012 and Suzuki 2014 both treat jar calls as a discrete Japanese tit mobbing-call type, distinct from chicka calls. The call is also used in later predation-risk playback work by Suzuki 2015.

calls.acoustic_description: A multi-note parid alarm call assembled from A, B, and C note units, often within the broader chicka-call system. Notes are short and ordered, and the number and arrangement of notes can vary across predator contexts. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in mobbing and danger contexts, especially around aerial or climbing nest predators such as crows and martens. Playback of ABC units causes receivers to scan the surroundings, particularly the horizontal field where such predators are expected.
calls.comments: Suzuki 2014 documents chicka calls in predator-presentation trials, and Suzuki, Wheatcroft, and Griesser 2016 experimentally separates the ABC unit from D notes. The label is strong, though ABC is a functional unit within a broader variable chicka-call family.

calls.acoustic_description: A string of repeated short D notes, usually delivered as a dee-like series. In experimental stimuli, D notes occur as multiple repeated elements rather than a single isolated note. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, harmonic, short, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Functions as an approach or recruitment signal. In playback experiments, receivers approach the caller or loudspeaker in response to D-note strings, and D notes add recruitment value when combined after ABC calls.
calls.comments: Suzuki, Wheatcroft, and Griesser 2016 identifies D-note strings as a meaningful call unit and Suzuki 2014 documents D notes within natural chicka-call combinations. The label is medium because D is often discussed as a note unit or subcall rather than a fully independent repertoire category.

calls.acoustic_description: An ordered compound call in which A, B, and C note units precede a repeated string of D notes. Natural intervals between note units are short, and reversing the order to D-ABC disrupts receiver interpretation. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, repetitive, multi component, long.
calls.semantic_description: Combines the danger-scanning response associated with ABC notes and the approach response associated with D notes. Receivers treat the natural ABC-D order as a compound signal that recruits them while they scan for danger.
calls.comments: Suzuki, Wheatcroft, and Griesser 2016 records natural ABC-D sequences and tests them experimentally, while Suzuki 2014 shows that Japanese tits use many structured chicka-note combinations in predator contexts. The natural ordered sequence is well supported.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Rudnai 1973 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is a wild field monograph on Nairobi National Park lions and includes a dedicated communication section covering vocalization and marking. Schaller 1972 provides a second classic wild field account from the Serengeti, and later peer-reviewed studies add quantitative and playback evidence mainly for roaring. This file includes wild-supported named call types from the classic field inventories where acoustic and contextual descriptions can be supported; cough is treated as a growl-like variant, and purr-like or captivity-only labels are not included without clear wild evidence. The recently named intermediate roar is included as an outside-inventory call because Growcott et al. 2025 provides direct wild acoustic evidence for it.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud low-frequency call produced in bouts. A typical bout contains introductory moans, several full-throated roar elements, and terminal grunts, with roar elements showing broad frequency contours and individually distinctive temporal structure. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, loud, long, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used over long distances for territorial advertisement, spacing between groups, locating or recruiting companions, and mate-related signalling. Playback studies show that listeners use roars to assess caller identity, group size, sex or status, and the risk posed by unfamiliar intruders.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 treat roaring as a core wild lion call, and Stander and Stander 1988, Pfefferle et al. 2007, Wijers et al. 2021a, and Growcott et al. 2025 analyze the same call class. Authors differ in how they split bout components, but the roar itself is uncontested.

calls.acoustic_description: A roar-bout element that is shorter and flatter in pitch contour than the full-throated roar. It follows full-throated roar elements within the bout and can be separated from them using simple duration and frequency measures. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, loud, short, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Occurs as part of the long-distance roaring bout used for territorial advertisement and intra-pride communication. Its independent contextual meaning has not yet been separated from the broader roaring-bout context.
calls.comments: Growcott et al. 2025 provides direct wild quantitative evidence and names the intermediate roar, but the category is new and has not yet been independently replicated in other lion populations or playback studies.

calls.acoustic_description: A comparatively soft, low-pitched, drawn-out call that can begin a roaring bout. It is less intense than the full-throated roar and grades into the louder bout elements. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, frequency modulated, long, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in the opening phase of long-distance roaring bouts and in close social situations described in classic field accounts. In bout use, it contributes to the same territorial, spacing, and contact context as roaring.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 name moans, and Grinnell and McComb 2001 and Growcott et al. 2025 describe moans as bout components. Agreement is medium because moans are often treated as part of a roaring sequence rather than as a separately tested call.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low, pulse-like call that may occur singly, in series, or as the terminal portion of a roaring bout. It is briefer and less resonant than the full-throated roar. Acoustic features: low frequency, pulsed, short, abrupt, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in close-range social contact and as the ending phase of roaring bouts. In bout sequences it participates in long-distance territorial and contact signalling; in close range it accompanies social approach or group movement.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 list grunts, and Grinnell and McComb 2001 and Growcott et al. 2025 recognize terminal grunts in roaring bouts. Agreement is medium because close-range grunts and terminal bout grunts may not be identical subtypes.

calls.acoustic_description: A low, rough, noisy call that may be sustained or broken into shorter growl-cough variants. It has a harsher broadband quality than moans or mews and can vary in intensity. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during close-range agonistic encounters, feeding disputes, defensive approach, and situations where another animal is being warned away. It functions as a threat or spacing signal.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 both include growl-like calls in wild lions, but later targeted acoustic work has focused on roaring rather than growls. The call type is accepted in classic inventories, with limited modern replication.

calls.acoustic_description: A harsh broadband call with abrupt noisy energy, often shorter and sharper than a sustained growl. It may grade acoustically with growls during intense close-range interactions. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given in close-range threat, defensive, or aggressive contexts, including responses to unfamiliar or threatening conspecifics. It accompanies escalation or attempted spacing of another animal.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 list snarling in wild lions, and McComb et al. 1993 records snarling as a response during roar playback experiments. Agreement is medium because snarl boundaries from growls are graded.

calls.acoustic_description: A noisy broadband close-range call complex. Hisses are more sustained and aperiodic, while spits are shorter and more explosive; both lack the low resonant structure of growls and roars. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in defensive or high-arousal close-range contexts, including by young animals and adults when threatened, cornered, or trying to deter approach. It draws attention to an immediate close-range conflict or disturbance.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 both include hiss or spit terms for wild lions. They are combined here because field descriptions treat them as closely related defensive noisy calls, and later lion-specific acoustic work has not separated them.

calls.acoustic_description: A relatively high-pitched tonal call with a clear harmonic trace and frequency modulation. It is shorter and quieter than roaring and less noisy than growls, hisses, or spits. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, short, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used in close-range contact and care contexts, especially between cubs and mothers, and during attention-seeking or separated-animal situations. Adults may also use mew-like calls during close social contact.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 describe mew-like calls in wild lions, especially in mother-cub communication. Later lion-specific acoustic studies largely ignore this close-range call type, so agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft, short, noisy exhaled sound, often given in repeated puffs. It is less resonant than grunts and lacks the harsh intensity of growls or snarls. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, quiet, pulsed, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Used in close-range affiliative or care-related interactions, including greetings or peaceful contact. It signals low-intensity social engagement rather than long-distance advertisement.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 support puffing as a wild close-range call. Agreement is medium because later lion-focused research has not examined puffing in detail and related felid literature sometimes uses different terms.

calls.acoustic_description: A short abrupt bark-like call with broadband energy and a low, forceful onset. It is briefer than a growl and not organized into the repeated low-frequency arc of a roaring bout. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Given in alert or disturbed contexts when a lion reacts to a nearby threat or unexpected stimulus. It can function as a short-range warning or attention signal.
calls.comments: Rudnai 1973 and Schaller 1972 both support woof-like alarm calls in wild lions. Agreement is medium because later acoustic studies do not target woofs and the label overlaps with bark-like descriptions.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Manser et al. 2014 is used as the peer-reviewed repertoire spine because it summarizes the wild adult meerkat vocal system across spatial coordination, antipredator behaviour, sentinel behaviour, affiliative interactions, and agonistic interactions, while citing Manser 1998 for the full thesis inventory of more than 30 call types. Because the thesis is not a peer-reviewed paper and the chapter gives some repertoire classes by count rather than naming every call type, this file includes only named wild call types with peer-reviewed acoustic and semantic support. Calls marked in_primary_inventory are call types or call classes explicitly covered by the 2014 spine; pup begging calls are retained as outside-inventory calls because the spine's count table is adult-focused.

calls.acoustic_description: A quiet, short-range contact call produced repeatedly during foraging. Close calls are individually variable and their rate and structure vary with caller traits, spacing to neighbours, social context, season, and wind, while remaining much softer and shorter than alarm, recruitment, or movement calls. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, quiet, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used during foraging and group movement to maintain cohesion, advertise local presence, and monitor nearby group members. Playback and field observations show that close calls can attract group members, elicit call feedback, and support spatial coordination rather than immediate predator response.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 treats close calls as a core spatial-coordination call, and Mausbach et al. 2017, Townsend et al. 2010, Reber et al. 2013, and Engesser and Manser 2022 independently study the same wild call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A conspicuous movement-coordination call that can be produced singly or as a chorus by several foraging group members. Published behavioural studies treat it as acoustically distinguishable from close calls and lead calls, but provide less spectrographic detail than the alarm or sentinel literature. Acoustic features: loud, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced before or during changes of foraging patch and during returns to sleeping burrows. Groups increase travel speed and are more likely to shift patches once several group members join the chorus, indicating a quorum-like group movement signal.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 lists distinct spatial-coordination calls in meerkats, and Bousquet et al. 2011 plus Gall et al. 2017 independently treat moving calls as a named call type separate from close and lead calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, loud alarm-call category whose acoustic structure varies with predator class and urgency. High-urgency variants become noisier and more abrupt, while lower-urgency variants are more harmonic; barks in aerial contexts include broadband formant structure. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when an aerial predator or flying predator-like threat is detected. Receivers use the call to select an escape response appropriate to aerial danger, with urgency level modulating the strength and immediacy of response.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 summarizes meerkat predator-specific alarm calls, Manser 2001 separates aerial alarms acoustically, Manser et al. 2001 tests receiver responses, and later bark and sentinel-sequence studies retain aerial predator context.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, short alarm-call category with urgency-dependent variation in noisiness, duration, and temporal patterning. It is acoustically separable from aerial and recruitment alarms, while within-category structure changes with response urgency. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced to terrestrial predators or ground-level threats. Receivers respond with ground-predator-appropriate vigilance, shelter use, or refuge behaviour, and urgency changes the intensity and speed of response.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 reviews predator-specific alarm calls, Manser 2001 identifies terrestrial alarms as a principal alarm category, and Manser et al. 2001 confirms that receivers treat predator classes differently.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud alarm-related call category with repeated noisy elements and urgency-dependent structural variation. It is acoustically separable from aerial and terrestrial alarm calls in Manser's predator-type analysis. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, loud, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used when the caller recruits group members toward a localized threat or cue, such as snakes, predator deposits, or other objects requiring inspection or mobbing, rather than simply triggering immediate flight.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 covers the meerkat alarm and recruitment system, Manser 2001 includes recruitment calls as a distinct alarm-call category, and Graw and Manser 2007 plus Zottl et al. 2013 independently describe recruitment during mobbing and direct predator-cue responses.

calls.acoustic_description: A broadband noisy call lacking clear fundamental-frequency and harmonic structure, with multiple formant bands below 15 kHz. Formant pattern differs among callers and the first formant varies between aerial and terrestrial predator contexts. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, loud, short, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly when meerkats detect aerial or terrestrial predators, with formant structure carrying potential information about caller identity and predator context. Barks may also occur rarely when individuals are isolated or lost, but the best-supported wild use is alarm.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 includes barks among meerkat call sequences and Townsend et al. 2014 provides a focused acoustic analysis of wild meerkat barks. The call type is independently recognizable in repertoire and acoustic work.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft sentinel-call unit composed of one short tonal note, often repeated during sentinel bouts. It is the lowest-risk end of the sentinel sequence gradation from single-note through alarm calls. Acoustic features: tonal, short, quiet, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given by sentinels during low perceived predation risk and used by foragers as social information that a guard is present. Together with double-note calls it functions as an all-clear or calming signal that reduces receiver vigilance and supports continued foraging.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 reports six sentinel calls; Rauber and Manser 2017, Rauber et al. 2020, and Rauber and Manser 2021 all identify the single-note call as one of the six discrete sentinel call types.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft sentinel-call unit composed of two short tonal notes. It is repeated in sentinel bouts, individually distinctive, and lies just above the single-note call in the graded sentinel sequence. Acoustic features: tonal, short, quiet, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given by sentinels during low perceived predation risk and used by foragers as an all-clear signal. Playbacks of calming calls reduce vigilance, and receiver responses vary with caller experience and social relationship.
calls.comments: The double-note call is one of the six sentinel calls reported in the repertoire spine and is repeatedly identified as a discrete type by Rauber and Manser 2017, Rauber et al. 2020, and Rauber and Manser 2021.

calls.acoustic_description: A short-note sentinel call composed of three tonal note units. It sits between double-note and multiple-note calls in the graded sequence of increasing perceived risk. Acoustic features: tonal, short, quiet, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by sentinels as perceived predation risk rises above the all-clear single- and double-note range but before the long warning calls. Sequence analyses indicate that it contributes to the graded encoding of subtle risk changes during guarding.
calls.comments: Triple-note calls are named among the six discrete sentinel types in Rauber and Manser 2017, Rauber et al. 2020, and Rauber and Manser 2021, matching the six-sentinel-call inventory summarized by Manser et al. 2014.

calls.acoustic_description: A short-note sentinel call composed of more than three tonal note units in a repeated note cluster. It occupies the upper part of the short-note sentinel gradation, just before di-drrr and wheek warning calls. Acoustic features: tonal, short, quiet, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by sentinels when perceived risk is elevated relative to single-, double-, and triple-note states but has not yet reached the long warning-call or full alarm-call range. It contributes to graded risk information in sentinel sequences.
calls.comments: Multiple-note calls are consistently listed as one of the six sentinel calls by Rauber and Manser 2017, Rauber et al. 2020, and Rauber and Manser 2021, and fall within the six-call sentinel class in Manser et al. 2014.

calls.acoustic_description: A longer, modulated sentinel warning call that follows the short-note calls in the graded sequence. It is structurally distinct from the note-counted single-, double-, triple-, and multiple-note calls. Acoustic features: frequency modulated, tonal, long, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when perceived predation risk is elevated but before an immediate predator-specific alarm is required. Together with wheek calls, it functions as a warning-side sentinel signal that increases receiver vigilance and reduces foraging.
calls.comments: Di-drrr calls are named as one of the six sentinel calls in Rauber and Manser 2017, Rauber et al. 2020, and Rauber and Manser 2021, matching the sentinel-call class summarized by Manser et al. 2014.

calls.acoustic_description: A longer, high, modulated sentinel warning call that follows di-drrr in the sentinel sequence and precedes full alarm calls at the high-risk end of the gradation. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, long, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when perceived predation risk is high but before or just below the threshold for a predator-specific alarm call. It is part of the warning call set that causes receivers to increase vigilance and reduce foraging.
calls.comments: Wheek calls are one of the six discrete sentinel call types in Rauber and Manser 2017, Rauber et al. 2020, and Rauber and Manser 2021, and sit within the six-sentinel-call repertoire class in Manser et al. 2014.

calls.acoustic_description: A repeated pup begging call produced in long bouts while dependent young accompany foraging adults. It is acoustically distinct from the louder high-pitched begging calls produced during feeding events, and its structure changes with age as young approach independence. Acoustic features: high frequency, short, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used by mobile dependent pups while following foraging adults. Call rate increases with hunger, adults allocate food in relation to repeat-call rate, and playbacks can provoke renewed provisioning after begging has naturally ceased.
calls.comments: Kunc et al. 2007 and Manser et al. 2008 explicitly distinguish repeat calls from high-pitched begging calls, and Madden et al. 2009 uses age-specific begging-call playbacks. The repeat call is a well-supported pup call type outside the adult inventory spine.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-frequency, more intense begging call that dependent young switch to when adults have food. It is acoustically distinct from repeat calls and is produced in vigorous bouts during feeding opportunities. Acoustic features: high frequency, loud, short, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Used by pups during direct feeding opportunities, especially when an adult has food available. Adults prefer high-pitched begging calls over repeat calls in feeding-choice experiments, although food allocation across longer periods tracks repeat-call rate more strongly.
calls.comments: Kunc et al. 2007 identifies high-pitched calls as a distinct begging call type used in a different social context from repeat calls, and Manser et al. 2008 retains the same two-call distinction.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft call produced in bouts of one or more short notes during morning sunning sessions near the burrow. Demartsev et al. 2018 classified single-, double-, triple-, and multiple-note sunning calls, with rare modulated variants excluded from their main analysis. Acoustic features: tonal, short, quiet, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced primarily during low-conflict sunning after emergence from the sleeping burrow. Calls are socially stimulated, coordinated by turn-taking that avoids overlap, and may support cooperative group interaction or bonding, though the precise function remains less certain than for alarm or close calls.
calls.comments: Manser et al. 2014 notes meerkat affiliative calls given while sunning, and Demartsev et al. 2018 provides a focused observational and playback study of specific sunning calls. Existence as a distinct call type is strong.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Ransom 1981 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is a primary field monograph on free-ranging olive baboons at Gombe and enumerates the named vocal classes most often repeated for this species: basic grunts, broken grunting, pant-grunts, roargrunts, cough-barks, cough-gecks, wa-hoos, shrill barks, screams, moans, basic gecks, and juvenile panting. Later wild olive baboon studies by Ey and Fischer 2011, Ey et al. 2009, Silk et al. 2018, and Bouquet et al. 2018 provide focused support for contact grunts, clear/contact and loud calls, and copulation calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-amplitude, low-frequency, harmonically structured grunt, usually produced as short elements singly or in bouts. Wild olive baboon studies show that grunt duration can lengthen in denser habitat, while the general grunt form remains conserved. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, short, quiet, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during routine feeding, travel, settling, close approaches, and affiliative social interactions. Female approach grunts in wild olive baboons predict less aggression and more affiliative interaction, including infant handling.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 lists basic grunts in the olive baboon repertoire, Ey et al. 2009 and Ey and Fischer 2011 analyze wild olive baboon grunts, Silk et al. 2018 studies their social use, and Hammerschmidt and Fischer 2019 treats grunts as a conserved Papio call type. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-volume, rapid series of short grunt elements. It is described as a broken, temporally segmented version of grunting rather than a single sustained call. Acoustic features: low frequency, short, quiet, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given during relatively low-intensity aggressive encounters, before or during interactions that may escalate. It is associated with tense social encounters rather than routine affiliation.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 names broken grunting for wild olive baboons, and the broader Papio literature recognizes rapid or graded grunt variants. Fewer olive-specific quantitative studies isolate it from other grunts, so existence agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A louder, repeated two-phase grunt with inhaled and exhaled components. The elements are short and pulsed, forming a faster and higher-amplitude bout than broken grunting. Acoustic features: low frequency, short, repetitive, pulsed, multi component, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when aggressive encounters intensify. It occurs in escalated social conflict and is treated as a higher-arousal continuation of lower-intensity grunting.
calls.comments: Pant-grunts are named in Ransom 1981 for wild olive baboons and correspond to widely recognized two-phase grunt variants in Papio, but they are not a main target of newer olive baboon acoustic work. Agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A deep, resonant male call built from low-pitched grunt-like or humming elements, often in a bout. The signal is lower and more sustained than ordinary grunts and can grade toward roar-like sound. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, long, loud, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given by adult males during displays, after fights, or during disturbances. It is associated with male arousal, threat, and social display contexts.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 lists roargrunts in wild olive baboons and comparative Papio work recognizes male loud-call and roargrunt classes. Olive-specific modern quantification is thinner than for ordinary grunts and loud calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, abrupt, cough-like bark with broadband noise. It is harsher than clear contact barks and lacks the extended two-syllable form of wa-hoos. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in low-anxiety alarm or disturbance contexts, including responses to unfamiliar humans or low-flying birds. It alerts nearby group members to a possible threat.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 names cough-barks for wild olive baboons. Later Papio work supports bark and loud-call classes broadly, but the cough-bark subtype is less often isolated in modern olive baboon studies.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, abrupt, cough-like geck, often described as a sharper and less bark-like noisy element than cough-barks. It can be given singly or in brief series. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in low-level alarm, anxiety, or discomfort contexts, including unfamiliar humans and low-flying birds. It is associated with orientation to possible external disturbance.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 lists cough-gecks in the wild olive baboon repertoire. The named type is clear in that inventory but less represented in later acoustic analyses.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud two-syllable call with an initial wa-like component followed by a lower hoo-like component. Bouts can contain repeated calls over extended periods and grade with other loud-call variants. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, multi component, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during predator or disturbance contexts, separation or attempts to regain group contact, night-time exchanges near sleeping sites, and male display or intergroup contexts.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 names wa-hoos for wild olive baboons, Ey 2008 and Ey and Fischer 2011 treat loud calls in wild Nigerian olive baboons, and Hammerschmidt and Fischer 2019 includes olive baboon loud calls in comparative Papio analyses. Existence is strongly supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, explosive bark with a sharp onset and relatively high-frequency noisy energy. Inventory and comparative accounts distinguish it from quieter grunts and from longer two-syllable wa-hoos. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given when a potential threat appears suddenly, including humans or predators. It can startle or orient other group members toward immediate danger.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 describes shrill barks in wild olive baboons, while Ey 2008 and Ey and Fischer 2011 document clear/contact bark and loud-call variants in wild olive baboons. Comparative Papio work also recognizes bark/loud-call classes.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, high-pitched, sustained or continuous call, often harsh or noisy. Scream bouts can vary in duration and intensity with arousal. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, long, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in highly stressful contexts, including pain, fear, aggression, and retreat during aggressive encounters. It is common across age and sex classes during intense social disturbance.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 names screams for wild olive baboons, and Hammerschmidt and Fischer 2019 treats screams as a major Papio call class separated from grunts and loud calls. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A comparatively soft, tonal immature call that is longer than a geck and can show gradual frequency modulation. It is described as a moaning call rather than a bark or grunt. Acoustic features: tonal, long, frequency modulated, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by infants and juveniles during discomfort, fear, separation from the mother, weaning, or tantrum-like episodes. It is associated with immature distress and caregiving contexts.
calls.comments: Moans are listed by Ransom 1981 as wild immature olive baboon calls. The inventory support is clear, but later olive baboon acoustic studies have focused mainly on adults and contact calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A brief, sharp, geck-like call with abrupt onset and noisy broadband structure. It can be produced singly or in short repetitions. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by infants and juveniles in discomfort, fear, frustration, separation from the mother, or weaning contexts. It is an immature distress and contact-maintenance call.
calls.comments: Basic gecks are named in Ransom 1981 for wild immature olive baboons. The call type is well supported by the primary inventory but has little later olive-specific acoustic analysis.

calls.acoustic_description: A breathy, repeated, pulsed call with short pant-like elements. It is less tonal and less bark-like than contact or alarm calls. Acoustic features: noisy, short, repetitive, pulsed, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by young olive baboons during rough-and-tumble play. It is associated with nonaggressive immature social play.
calls.comments: Ransom 1981 lists juvenile panting as a wild olive baboon call. Later olive baboon studies rarely focus on this immature play call, so agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A conspicuous female mating-associated call, typically described as a distinct call sequence rather than a single quiet grunt. Olive-specific publications emphasize occurrence and function more than fine acoustic structure. Acoustic features: loud, repetitive, multi component, graded, noisy.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by sexually receptive females during or shortly after copulation. In wild olive baboons, calling probability after mounts has been modeled against hypotheses involving sperm competition, male competition, and female choice.
calls.comments: Bouquet et al. 2018 provides direct wild olive baboon evidence for female copulation calls, and Hammerschmidt and Fischer 2019 recognizes copulation calls as a Papio call type. The call is not marked as in_primary_inventory because the Ransom 1981 spine sources consulted for this file did not clearly enumerate it.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2006 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the central wild study of adult male putty-nosed monkey alarm calling at Gashaka Gumti National Park, identifying pyows, hacks, and structured call series in response to predator stimuli. It is not a complete all-age/sex repertoire inventory, so this file supplements it with later wild studies for female chirps, male keks/short pyows, caller identity, and cross-population call ordering. Broad secondary-only or captivity-only call labels are excluded.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud adult-male call that is more acoustically variable than hacks, with tonal structure and descending frequency modulation reported from about 2.5 kHz toward lower frequencies. Pyows are commonly produced in repeated series and contain individually distinctive acoustic cues. Acoustic features: tonal, frequency modulated, loud, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males across a broad range of disturbance contexts, including terrestrial threats such as leopards, calls from other males, intergroup situations, and situations in which the cause is not obvious to listeners. Females can use pyow-associated cues to recognize male identity during antipredator contexts.
calls.comments: Pyows are one of the two central male call types in Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2006, recur in predator-model and playback work by Arnold et al. 2008 and Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2013, and are analyzed for identity cues by Price et al. 2009 and Kiminou et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, short, low-frequency adult-male call with abrupt onset, often repeated in series. Published descriptions place the major band of acoustic energy around 0.6-1.1 kHz and distinguish hacks from the longer, more variable descending pyows. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, short, abrupt, loud, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced especially in response to crowned eagle-related stimuli and other disturbances. Receivers treat hack series without additional contextual cues as evidence for aerial danger, but natural production also includes non-eagle contexts, so the call is not narrowly predator-specific.
calls.comments: Hacks are the second central male call type in Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2006 and are retained as a distinct alarm playback class in Arnold et al. 2008, Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2013, Kiminou et al. 2022, and Mehon et al. 2024. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A very short adult-male alarm call, reported with durations around 0.04-0.06 s and major acoustic energy spread from roughly 0.5 to 3 kHz. Keks lack the descending frequency transition typical of long pyows and resemble the short-pyow category described in other populations. Acoustic features: short, abrupt, broadband, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by males during close-range terrestrial threat encounters, especially when a leopard model has been visually detected and the male engages in predator defence or mobbing. Later cross-population work treats keks or short pyows as one of the basic male call types used in leopard contexts.
calls.comments: Mehon and Stephan 2021 report keks as a newly documented male alarm, Kiminou et al. 2022 uses keks in wild playback tests, and Mehon et al. 2024 links keks with the short-pyow category across populations. Agreement is medium because the label is newer and partly reconciles population terminology.

calls.acoustic_description: A short female alarm call identified in wild studies as a single chirp-type call. Published work provides less quantitative acoustic detail than for male pyows, hacks, and keks, but spectrographic illustrations and playback/production studies treat it as a distinct female alarm class. Acoustic features: high frequency, short, abrupt, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by females as a general alarm to threatening events. During predator-defence experiments, female chirps recruit the group male, after which females may reduce their own alarm calling when male calls associated with direct defence are produced.
calls.comments: Mehon and Stephan 2021 identify a single female chirp alarm in wild putty-nosed monkeys, and Kiminou et al. 2022 summarizes females as possessing one general chirp alarm. Existence agreement is medium because the detailed literature is recent and narrower than for male calls.

calls.acoustic_description: An ordered multi-call sequence in which a small number of pyows precedes a small number of hacks, commonly described as 1-4 pyows followed by 1-4 hacks. The sequence combines the acoustic units of pyows and hacks into a stereotyped order rather than forming a new single-note call. Acoustic features: multi component, repetitive, tonal, frequency modulated, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in predatory and non-predatory contexts and reliably associated with forthcoming group progression in the best-studied population. Playback experiments show that receivers move after hearing pyow-hack sequences, especially when produced by their own group male.
calls.comments: The pyow-hack sequence is described by Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2006, experimentally tested by Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2008, discussed in Arnold and Zuberbuhler 2013, and revisited by Schlenker et al. 2016. Existence agreement is strong for the Gashaka system.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Collias 1987 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the only species-level spectrographic inventory for red junglefowl, describing 24 vocal signals from an unconfined color-banded flock and comparing them with wild and domestic Gallus evidence. This file retains the named call types that are supported by Collias 1987 and by native-field or red-junglefowl-focused studies, especially Collias and Collias 1967 for crowing, courtship/food calling, clucking, alarm calls, and chick calls. It does not enumerate Collias's comfort, pain, mild-disturbance, and closely graded captivity-associated categories when wild contextual evidence is sparse.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud stereotyped male call with three or four note-like energy peaks, clear harmonic structure, and some harsh energy. Red junglefowl crows are shorter and less drawn out than many domestic-fowl crows, with the strongest energy commonly concentrated near the third note. Acoustic features: loud, harmonic, multi component, long, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly by adult males around roosts at dawn, with a smaller evening peak, and also during territorial and dominance interactions. Field observations treat it as a spacing, territorial, dominance, and mate-attraction signal.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 treats crowing as the species- and sex-specific adult male call, Collias and Collias 1967 document it extensively in native Indian field observations, and Hao et al. 2022 and Hao et al. 2025 provide modern red-junglefowl acoustic and activity data for male vocalization.

calls.acoustic_description: A low-amplitude series of brief, rapidly repeated notes or pulses, often rendered as kuk- or tik-like elements. In the inventory it can deepen and accelerate during close female-directed display and may grade toward the nest-site attraction call. Acoustic features: short, repetitive, low frequency, pulsed, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by males around food items, food-like objects, or potential courtship opportunities in the presence of females. Females may approach the male, and the display can precede feeding by the female or mating.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 lists the food call and courtship call by males, Collias and Collias 1967 describe the same wild male attraction call in field observations, and Stokes 1971 treats parental and courtship feeding in red junglefowl as a focal behavior.

calls.acoustic_description: A rapid train of brief low-pitched notes, structurally close to the male food call but associated in the inventory with nest-site display. The notes are short, low, and repeated in a dense sequence. Acoustic features: short, repetitive, low frequency, quiet, pulsed.
calls.semantic_description: Given by adult males to attract hens to a potential nest site during courtship and pair interactions. It is treated as part of the male attraction-call set rather than as a general contact call.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 explicitly names a nest-site attraction call, and Stokes 1971 supports the broader red-junglefowl courtship-feeding system. Agreement is medium because the category is close to the male food/courtship call and is not separately emphasized in the native field study.

calls.acoustic_description: A series of soft brief notes, usually single rather than paired, repeated at a relatively rapid and irregular rate. The notes emphasize lower frequencies and are less drawn out than clucking or purring. Acoustic features: short, repetitive, low frequency, pulsed, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by broody females when directing chicks to food, often with food handling or pecking movements. Chicks respond by approaching, reducing ongoing calling, or changing movement and feeding behavior.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 includes the hen food call, Sherry 1977 experimentally studies parental food calling in Burmese red junglefowl, and Snapp 1969 shows red-junglefowl chicks discriminate maternal feeding calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft repeated series of brief low-frequency notes, often paired as cluck units. The paired-note structure distinguishes it from the more rapid single-note maternal food call. Acoustic features: short, repetitive, low frequency, quiet, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Used by broody females while moving with chicks and maintaining brood cohesion. Field observations describe hens leading chicks with clucking sounds.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 lists clucking by broody hens, and Collias and Collias 1967 report clucking in wild hen-chick movements. The call is a standard maternal red-junglefowl category.

calls.acoustic_description: A harsh cackling series with short abrupt notes spread over a wide frequency range, often including rhythmically repeated cut-like notes and louder harsh terminal elements. It has broader and higher-frequency energy than low threat calls. Acoustic features: loud, broadband, noisy, abrupt, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when a predator or disturbing animal is on the ground or perched nearby and immediate escape is not the only response. Field observations describe it as alerting and scolding around discovered predators.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 names warning calls to ground or perched predators, and Collias and Collias 1967 report cackling alarm cries in wild red junglefowl, including around a perched serpent eagle and around human disturbance.

calls.acoustic_description: A very loud harsh scream with strong high-frequency energy and a more gradual onset than the explosive ground-predator notes. Some calls include both high-frequency alarm energy and lower-frequency components. Acoustic features: loud, high frequency, broadband, noisy, long, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Given during sudden high-risk predator events, especially aerial attacks or similar emergencies. Field observations describe it as a high-intensity call that can silence other vocalizing and calls for immediate action.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 describes the warning scream to flying predators, and Collias and Collias 1967 identify the wild high-intensity hawk-call category. The aerial/emergency alarm is a stable named call type.

calls.acoustic_description: Very loud harsh squawks with broad frequency spread, abrupt onset, long notes, and broken or wavering harmonic streaks. The notes are louder and longer than ordinary pain or startle cries and can be repeated. Acoustic features: loud, broadband, noisy, abrupt, long, repetitive.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adults during capture or intense restraint. It is associated with immediate distress and can serve as alarm information to nearby conspecifics.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 names adult distress squawks from captured birds, and Snapp 1969 supports red-junglefowl chick discrimination of adult distress calls. The call is well recognized, but much of the detailed adult evidence is from handling contexts.

calls.acoustic_description: A harsh low-frequency call with broad frequency energy but emphasis below the high-frequency alarm band. It can be lower in intensity than predator alarm calls and may grade into louder roar-like threat sounds. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, broadband, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during close aggressive or defensive interactions, including contests, dominance encounters, and defensive postures. It can accompany physical orientation toward an opponent and may precede pecking or withdrawal.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 names threat calls by both sexes and relates them to low-frequency harsh structure; Collias and Collias 1967 document natural dominance and territorial interactions where such aggressive signaling occurs. Agreement is medium because threat calls are graded and partly overlap with roar-like defensive calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-pitched juvenile call made from repeated descending frequency cycles or trilled elements. Fear trills include irregular and very high-frequency components, while separation distress cries are loud and strident. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, repetitive, loud, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by chicks during separation, capture, threat, or insecurity. Field observations report similar loud chick distress cries in wild red junglefowl, especially when chicks are separated from the parent.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 describes chick distress cries and fear trills, Collias and Collias 1967 report chick distress cries in wild red junglefowl, and Snapp 1969 studies red-junglefowl chick responses to adult call categories. The juvenile distress category is well supported.

calls.acoustic_description: A softer juvenile call with repeated notes or cycles that tend to rise in average frequency, including chevron-like brood-contact notes with both rising and falling components. It is lower in intensity and more regular than chick fear trills. Acoustic features: frequency modulated, tonal, repetitive, quiet, short.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by chicks during feeding, brooding, or secure brood contact. It is associated with close interaction with the mother rather than separation or threat.
calls.comments: Collias 1987 separates chick pleasure trills and brood-contact notes in the inventory, while Collias and Collias 1967 supports similar soft chick calls in wild red junglefowl. The combined call entry is medium because the inventory distinguishes several juvenile secure-contact variants.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Rowell and Hinde 1962 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the classic spectrographic repertoire treatment of rhesus macaque vocal communication, separating clear calls from harsh calls and naming the main social call classes. Later free-ranging Cayo Santiago work by Hauser and Marler, Gouzoules and colleagues, and Partan is used to refine food-call, scream-subtype, and multimodal social contexts. This file includes named call types with wild or free-ranging support and excludes call labels whose detailed evidence is primarily captive-only.

calls.acoustic_description: A clear, narrowband tonal call with visible harmonic structure and most energy concentrated in the low harmonics. The frequency contour varies among callers and contexts, but food-associated and nonfood coos are reported to be acoustically very similar. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, long, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in contact contexts, including group progression, mother-infant separation, and some food discoveries. Playback studies show that adult females can recognize individual and kinship information in contact calls, and food-call studies show coos can accompany lower-quality food discoveries.
calls.comments: Rowell and Hinde 1962 list coos in the clear-call repertoire, Hauser and Marler 1993a treats coos as one of five food-associated calls in free-living rhesus macaques, and Rendall et al. 1996 uses contact calls in free-ranging playback experiments. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A low, atonal or weakly voiced call with pulsed structure, unstable fundamental frequency, and strong low-frequency energy bands. Food grunts and nonfood grunts are similar to the ear but differ measurably in several acoustic parameters. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, pulsed, short, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when individuals encounter lower-quality or common foods, especially provisioned chow, and also in nonfood social contexts such as grooming or close-range interactions. Food-call playbacks can attract other group members toward the caller.
calls.comments: Grunts are part of the older repertoire tradition summarized by Rowell and Hinde 1962 and are a central food-call class in Hauser and Marler 1993a and Hauser 1998. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A clear tonal food call with harmonic structure and a modulated frequency contour. It is acoustically distinct from harmonic arches and grunts, although receivers can perceptually group warbles with harmonic arches in food-call playback experiments. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by free-living rhesus macaques on discovering rare, high-quality foods such as coconut. Receivers hearing food-call playbacks typically approach, and habituation experiments indicate that warbles are classified with other high-quality-food calls.
calls.comments: Warbles are included in the Rowell and Hinde 1962 repertoire and are repeatedly analyzed as one of the five free-ranging food-call classes by Hauser and Marler 1993a and Hauser 1998. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A clear tonal food call with harmonic structure and an arch-shaped frequency contour in which frequency rises and falls over the call. It is acoustically distinct from warbles and chirps but is perceptually grouped with warbles by receivers in field playback experiments. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced on discovery of rare, highly preferred foods. Playback and habituation experiments show that listeners treat harmonic arches as members of the high-quality-food call set and often respond by approaching the caller.
calls.comments: Harmonic arches are one of the five food-call classes in Hauser and Marler 1993a and are central to Hauser 1998 field playback tests. They are marked outside the primary inventory because the label is a later food-call refinement rather than the Rowell and Hinde 1962 spine label.

calls.acoustic_description: A short clear food call, acoustically distinct from coos, grunts, warbles, and harmonic arches. The call is brief and tonal compared with the noisier harsh calls in the repertoire. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, short, abrupt, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when free-living rhesus macaques discover rare, high-quality foods. It belongs to the food-call set that can bring listeners toward a food finder.
calls.comments: Chirps are named in Rowell and Hinde 1962 and are one of the five free-ranging food-call classes in Hauser and Marler 1993a and Hauser 1998. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A harsh, abrupt broadband vocalization with noisy energy spread across frequencies. In free-ranging multimodal observations, barks were associated with a stereotyped facial and head posture rather than the mouth shapes used for clear calls. Acoustic features: broadband, noisy, short, abrupt, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in threatening or aggressive social encounters. Free-ranging observations link barks with visual displays such as retracted ears and lowered head, supporting its use in close-range agonistic signalling.
calls.comments: Bark is named in the Rowell and Hinde 1962 repertoire and appears in Partan 2002 free-ranging multimodal analyses. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A repeated, breathy, weakly voiced harsh call that is longer and less voiced than a grunt. It is formed from pant-like pulses and can grade toward other low noisy aggressive calls. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, repetitive, pulsed, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by dominant animals toward subordinates in aggressive situations. Free-ranging multimodal work associates pant-threats with forward ears and raised head during agonistic displays.
calls.comments: Hauser and Marler 1993a distinguishes pant-threats acoustically from grunts, and Partan 2002 identifies pant-threats as a free-ranging vocal component tied to a specific visual display pattern. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft clear call with tonal or warbling elements, often produced in short repeated bouts. Free-ranging recordings link the vocal component to a stereotyped lip-smacking facial movement. Acoustic features: tonal, harmonic, quiet, repetitive, frequency modulated.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during close-range friendly or appeasing social interactions. Free-ranging multimodal observations report that girneys are accompanied by lipsmacking, supporting use in affiliative or low-tension social contact.
calls.comments: Girney-like calls are part of the Rowell and Hinde 1962 repertoire and are explicitly identified in Partan 2002 free-ranging multimodal observations. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud scream with broad noisy energy and little stable tonal structure. It is one of the five acoustically distinct recruitment scream classes described from free-ranging rhesus macaques. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, loud, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by victims during agonistic encounters, especially in contexts involving contact aggression from higher-ranking opponents. Playback work shows that mothers can respond differentially to scream information in the absence of other cues.
calls.comments: Gouzoules et al. 1984 identifies noisy screams as one of five acoustically distinct free-ranging recruitment scream classes, and Gouzoules et al. 1998 retains the class in later analyses of dominance and conflict severity. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, tonal scream with a sharply rising and then falling frequency contour, often forming one or more arch-shaped peaks. It is shorter and broader in bandwidth than tonal screams in comparative psychophysical descriptions. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, loud, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during agonistic encounters as part of the recruitment-scream system. The class is associated with particular opponent and aggression categories rather than simply with undifferentiated arousal.
calls.comments: Arched screams are a named class in Gouzoules et al. 1984 and were used as a perceptual class in Le Prell et al. 2002. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A long tonal scream with a clear fundamental-frequency contour and a distinctive tonal mid-section. Compared with arched screams, tonal screams are longer, lower in frequency, and narrower in bandwidth. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, loud, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in agonistic encounters as a recruitment scream, especially in non-contact aggression contexts involving higher-ranking opponents. It encodes aspects of the social conflict rather than only caller arousal.
calls.comments: Tonal screams are named by Gouzoules et al. 1984, used in Gouzoules et al. 1998 analyses, and tested against arched screams in Le Prell et al. 2002. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A scream composed of short pulses, with individual pulses ranging from noisy to more tonal structure. Later acoustic work describes pulsed screams as shorter than tonal screams and often less stable in tonality. Acoustic features: high frequency, pulsed, repetitive, short, noisy, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during agonistic encounters as part of the recruitment-scream set. The class contributes information about the opponent and aggression event in combination with other scream classes.
calls.comments: Pulsed screams are one of the five Gouzoules et al. 1984 free-ranging scream classes and are retained in later acoustic analyses such as Le Prell et al. 2002 and Fishell et al. 2022. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A long tonal scream with repeated up-and-down frequency modulation and several harmonic bands. It is one of the five scream classes separated from noisy, arched, tonal, and pulsed screams. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, harmonic, frequency modulated, long, loud.
calls.semantic_description: Produced during agonistic recruitment contexts, especially non-contact aggression in later analyses of rank-difference encounters. It helps encode features of the conflict and likely opponent class.
calls.comments: Undulating or undulated screams are named in Gouzoules et al. 1984 and retained in Gouzoules et al. 1998 as one of the five recruitment scream classes. Existence agreement is strong.

taxonomy_basis.summary: No dedicated peer-reviewed paper was found that supersedes the classic repertoire catalog. Kruuk 1972 is used as the spine because it is the original detailed inventory of named spotted hyena calls with acoustic notes, postures, and contexts; Hayssen and Noonan 2021 cite the Kruuk appendix and Mills 1990 table as the extensive catalog for the species. All named Kruuk inventory entries are included here, and no outside-inventory calls are added where later sources give only broad labels without call-level acoustic and semantic detail.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud tonal call given in bouts of repeated, discrete whoop units separated by pauses. Units typically begin low and sweep upward, and bouts can contain structurally distinct whoop types with stable individual acoustic signatures that carry over long distances. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, loud, repetitive, multi component.
calls.semantic_description: Used for medium- and long-distance communication when clan members are separated or need to coordinate. It advertises caller identity and location, requests or rallies support, and is used in contexts such as locating offspring, agonistic encounters, resource defense, and interclan interactions.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists whoops in the primary inventory, East and Hofer 1991a,b provide the classic structural and functional studies, and Theis et al. 2007 and Lehmann et al. 2022 analyze the same long-distance call in wild hyenas. Multiple independent studies agree that the whoop is a central discrete call type.

calls.acoustic_description: A whoop-like bout with shorter intervals and generally higher-pitched, more rapidly delivered elements than ordinary slow whooping. It grades toward the ordinary whoop but differs in rate, pitch, and arousal-related structure. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, loud, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in excited conflict contexts, especially with other hyenas present before attacks or during disputes over kills with lions, rival hyenas, or other competitors. It appears to recruit or coordinate nearby animals in high-arousal agonistic situations.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists fast whoop as a primary-inventory entry and Mills 1990 retains the inventory tradition, but Theis et al. 2007 discusses fast whoops as an arousal-related category within broader whooping. The call type is recognized, while its boundary from slow whoop is graded.

calls.acoustic_description: A soft, low-pitched growling sound lasting several seconds and audible only at close range. It is quieter and less far carrying than whoops or giggles and has a rougher, less tonal quality than groans. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, long, quiet.
calls.semantic_description: Given at close range during the approach of an unwelcome hyena or in tense social encounters, often before chasing or escalation. It functions as a low-level agonistic or spacing signal.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists grunt as a primary-inventory call, Mills 1990 uses the related soft-growl terminology, and Mathevon et al. 2010 cites the grunt or soft growl as a close-range call. Agreement is medium because labels vary and the category is close to groans and growls.

calls.acoustic_description: A low, sustained ooo-like close-range call, generally more tonal and rounded than the grunt. Experimental work shows groans can vary from growl-like to more prolonged tonal forms with higher fundamental frequency in some eliciting conditions. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, harmonic, long, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced before and during meeting or greeting ceremonies and also in adult-cub den interactions. It is associated with close social approach, greeting, and affiliative or caregiving contact rather than long-distance recruitment.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists groan as a primary-inventory call, Mills 1990 preserves the catalog, and Theunissen et al. 2008 experimentally elicited and analyzed groans. Agreement is medium because groans form a broad category that grades toward growls.

calls.acoustic_description: A usually low-pitched ooo-like call lasting several seconds. It is less bout-structured than whooping and is treated as a graded arousal call rather than a sharply bounded tonal display. Acoustic features: low frequency, tonal, long, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by aroused hyenas in situations resembling fast-whoop contexts but with less immediate attack tendency, including tense feeding or social conflicts. It appears to bring nearby group members into a shared state of arousal or readiness.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists low as a primary-inventory call, Mills 1990 retains the catalog, and Hayssen and Noonan 2021 includes lows in the species' vocal repertoire. Agreement is medium because later quantitative work has not focused on lows as a separate acoustic class.

calls.acoustic_description: A high-pitched staccato series of short notes, often produced in brief bouts with strong frequency and temporal variation. Acoustic parameters encode age, dominance-related status, and individual cues. Acoustic features: high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, short, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in close-range, high-arousal social situations, especially feeding competition, being chased, threatened, or attacked. It is associated with distress, frustration, or submission rather than amusement and may provide receivers with information about the caller's social position.
calls.comments: Giggles are listed in Kruuk 1972 and Mills 1990, included by Hayssen and Noonan 2021, and are the focus of Mathevon et al. 2010. The call is widely recognized as one of the characteristic spotted hyena vocalizations.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, high-pitched call lasting several seconds. It is more sustained and intense than individual giggle notes and lacks the repeated staccato bout structure of giggling. Acoustic features: high frequency, loud, long, abrupt, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in the same broad fleeing or attack context as giggles, but especially when the caller is actually being bitten. It functions as an acute distress signal during close-range aggression.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists yell as a primary-inventory call, Mills 1990 retains the catalog, and Hayssen and Noonan 2021 includes yells and related high-intensity calls in the repertoire. Agreement is medium because later work provides little call-specific quantification and broad accounts sometimes use scream-like labels.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, low, rattling broadband call lasting several seconds, with harsh noisy energy rather than the tonal structure of whoops or groans. It is one of the more forceful short-range aggressive sounds. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, loud, long, abrupt.
calls.semantic_description: Given in defensive or attack-related confrontations, especially when under attack or before retaliatory biting. It communicates high-intensity agonistic motivation at close range.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists growl as a primary-inventory call, Mills 1990 retains the aggressive-call catalog, and Hayssen and Noonan 2021 includes growls in the species repertoire. The label is medium because growls, grunts, and groans can grade into each other.

calls.acoustic_description: A rapid succession of low-pitched, soft, staccato grunt elements lasting several seconds. It has a pulsed repetitive structure but is quieter and lower than the giggle. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, short, quiet, repetitive, pulsed.
calls.semantic_description: Produced when fleeing in surprise from lions or humans and also when attacking large prey. It is associated with sudden danger, conflict, or high-arousal predatory encounters at close range.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists soft grunt-laugh as a primary-inventory call and Mills 1990 retains the catalog. Agreement is medium because later peer-reviewed accounts rarely analyze this call separately from other short-range high-arousal calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A louder and often much longer version of the grunt-laugh, built from repeated low-pitched grunt-like elements. It is still not as far carrying as whoops and may continue in extended bouts. Acoustic features: low frequency, noisy, long, repetitive, pulsed, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced in intense encounters with lions or other hyena clans. It is associated with group-level conflict, threat, and coordinated arousal during interspecific or interclan confrontation.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists loud grunt-laugh as a primary-inventory call and Mills 1990 retains the catalog. Agreement is medium because the category is probably graded with soft grunt-laughs and other agonistic calls.

calls.acoustic_description: A loud, high-pitched, rapid, drawn-out squealing whine, often repeated. It has a longer, more continuous quality than the staccato giggle and is harsher or more insistent than the soft squeal. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, long, loud, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used mainly by cubs when following a female before suckling or when prevented from obtaining food. It signals need, frustration, or distress in dependent young.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists whine as a primary-inventory call, Mills 1990 retains the catalog, and Hayssen and Noonan 2021 discusses juvenile vocalizations and the broader vocal repertoire. The label is medium because later quantitative work rarely isolates whines.

calls.acoustic_description: A softer high-pitched squeal related to the whine but without the same rapid staccato or insistent quality. It is a close-range call with a smoother, quieter delivery than the whine. Acoustic features: high frequency, tonal, long, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Used by both cubs and adults when encountering a clan mate after a long separation. It signals close-range reunion or appeasing social contact rather than immediate attack or long-distance recruitment.
calls.comments: Kruuk 1972 lists soft squeal as a primary-inventory call and Mills 1990 retains the catalog. Agreement is medium because later work often discusses high-pitched cub or reunion calls without separating this call quantitatively from whines.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Rand and Ryan 1981 is used as the repertoire spine because it is a peer-reviewed, species-specific inventory paper that frames the male advertisement call as a variable complexity series: a long whine followed by 0-6 chucks. I found a secondary/field-guide mention of a release call, but not peer-reviewed evidence with enough acoustic and semantic detail to add it under the current inclusion rules.

calls.acoustic_description: A single extended harmonic whine with a descending frequency-modulated contour, described in later studies as lasting roughly 350-400 ms and sweeping from about 900-400 Hz, with no terminal chuck components. It is the less complex end of the species' advertisement-call series. Acoustic features: low frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males at breeding pools and in choruses to attract females. Isolated males commonly give whine-only calls, and females can use the whine as a conspecific mate-attraction signal and species-recognition cue even though they often prefer calls with added chucks.
calls.comments: Rand and Ryan 1981 describe the advertisement call as a whine with 0-6 chucks, explicitly including the whine-only form, and Ryan 1983 plus Ryan and Rand 1990 treat the whine as a core component of sexual communication in this species. Multiple primary studies therefore agree that whine-only calls occur as a recognizable signal form.

calls.acoustic_description: A graded, multi-component advertisement call that begins with the same long descending harmonic whine and is followed by one or more short amplitude-modulated, multi-harmonic chuck bursts. Published descriptions report up to seven chucks of roughly 40 ms each, with chuck energy concentrated above 1.5 kHz and peaking near 2.3-2.4 kHz. Acoustic features: low frequency, high frequency, frequency modulated, tonal, harmonic, long, short, pulsed, multi component, repetitive, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced by adult males in breeding choruses, especially when other males are calling nearby or a receptive female is present. Females preferentially approach complex calls in phonotaxis tests, and males also call more in response to chuck-bearing calls, while males appear to balance the increased attractiveness and competitive value of chucks against ecological costs such as eavesdropping predators.
calls.comments: The whine-chuck call is the classic complex call in Rand and Ryan 1981, Ryan 1980, Ryan 1983, Ryan and Rand 1990, Ryan et al. 1990, and Bernal et al. 2009. These independent studies consistently identify the chuck-bearing form as a discrete complex variant of the advertisement call, even though the number of chucks grades from one to several.

taxonomy_basis.summary: Struhsaker 1967 is used as the primary_inventory spine because it is the classic observational and spectrographic inventory of free-ranging Amboseli vervet auditory communication. It enumerates the predator alarms and the major intragroup, intergroup, submissive, affiliative, play, and infant vocal or audible signal classes later summarized by Isbell and Enstam-Jaffe 2013 and Radick 2006. This file includes those named communicative call/sound classes, while excluding noncommunicative physiological noises such as coughs, sneezes, and vomiting.

calls.acoustic_description: A short, low-intensity alarm vocalization, named onomatopoetically by Struhsaker. Detailed spectrographic measurements are sparse, but inventory accounts distinguish it from louder, repeated, high-intensity alarm calls such as rraups, chirps, and threat-alarm barks. Acoustic features: low frequency, short, abrupt, quiet, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced to nearby minor terrestrial threats, including small mammalian predators or other low-intensity disturbances. It appears to alert group members to inspect the source of danger rather than to trigger the more urgent escape responses associated with major predators.
calls.comments: Struhsaker 1967 lists uh among the alarm-call repertoire and Radick 2006 discusses it as part of Struhsaker's broader predator-call table, but later experimental work focuses mostly on leopard, eagle, and snake alarm classes. The existence label is therefore medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A moderate-intensity, abrupt alarm call represented by the onomatopoetic label nyow. It is described as distinct from both the quieter uh and the higher-intensity rraup, chirp, and bark calls, but it has not received the same quantitative acoustic treatment as the classic three predator alarms. Acoustic features: short, loud, abrupt, noisy, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Given to sudden movements or appearances of minor predators such as baboons or small cats. It functions as an alerting call associated with moderate threat, often prompting orientation and sometimes flight.
calls.comments: Nyow is part of the Struhsaker 1967 alarm inventory and is repeated in later repertoire summaries, but it is not a central unit in the later playback and quantitative alarm-call literature. Existence agreement is medium.

calls.acoustic_description: A staccato, multi-element broadband call. Quantitative analyses identify high-frequency clusters of short elements, but also show graded continuity from typical chutters toward rraup-like calls when aggressive contexts are included. Acoustic features: high frequency, broadband, noisy, short, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced to snakes, especially pythons, and to some human or intergroup threats. Playback studies show snake-alarm responses such as looking down or inspecting the ground, while later analyses show that chutter-like calls also occur during between-group aggression.
calls.comments: Chutters are listed in Struhsaker 1967, experimentally tested as snake alarms by Seyfarth et al. 1980, acoustically analyzed by Owren and Bernacki 1988, and reanalyzed quantitatively by Price et al. 2015. Existence agreement is strong.

calls.acoustic_description: A rough, low-frequency alarm call, often produced as short noisy elements. Price et al. 2015 places rraups in lower-frequency clusters than typical chutters, while noting continuous intermediates between rraup-like and chutter-like calls in aggressive contexts. Acoustic features: low frequency, broadband, noisy, short, repetitive, multi component, graded.
calls.semantic_description: Produced mainly to aerial predators such as martial eagles. Playbacks elicit aerial-predator responses, including looking upward or moving toward cover, although rraup-like calls can also occur during escalated aggression.
